Clinical Identification

The 10-year-old child with high-grade fever, pain in the ear (otalgia), and likely ear discharge or reduced hearing — consistent with Acute Otitis Media (AOM). Common in children due to short, horizontal Eustachian tube.

Definition

Acute otitis media (AOM) is an acute infection of the middle ear, presenting with rapid onset of ear pain, fever, and otoscopic findings of bulging, opaque, erythematous tympanic membrane with reduced mobility.

Etiology

Organism Frequency
Streptococcus pneumoniae25–50% — most common bacterial cause
Haemophilus influenzae (non-typeable)20–30%
Moraxella catarrhalis10–15%
Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep)5–10%
Respiratory virusesRSV, influenza, parainfluenza, adenovirus — 40–70% (often co-infection with bacteria)
Staphylococcus aureus (incl. MRSA)5% (increasing)
Pseudomonas aeruginosaRare in AOM; common in chronic otitis, swimmer's ear

Pathogenesis

  1. Eustachian tube dysfunction — upper respiratory tract infection causes oedema → tube obstruction → negative pressure in middle ear → fluid accumulation.
  2. Aspiration of nasopharyngeal flora — bacteria enter middle ear through Eustachian tube; multiply in fluid → purulent infection.
  3. Inflammation — bulging, erythematous TM; pain; fever.
  4. TM rupture — may occur, with purulent ear discharge (otorrhoea); usually heals spontaneously.

Risk Factors

  • Age <2 years (short, horizontal Eustachian tube).
  • Day care attendance.
  • Tobacco smoke exposure (passive smoking).
  • Bottle feeding (especially supine); pacifier use.
  • Family history of otitis media.
  • Craniofacial abnormalities — cleft palate, Down syndrome.
  • Immunodeficiency.
  • Allergy.
  • Adenoid hypertrophy.

Clinical Features

  • Symptoms:
    • Otalgia (ear pain) — tugging at ear in infants.
    • Fever (often 38.5–40 °C).
    • Irritability, crying, poor feeding in infants.
    • Hearing loss, sensation of fullness in ear.
    • Otorrhoea (if TM ruptures) — purulent ear discharge; pain may suddenly decrease.
    • Headache, vomiting.
    • Preceding upper respiratory tract infection symptoms (cough, rhinorrhoea).
  • Otoscopic findings:
    • Bulging, erythematous, opaque tympanic membrane.
    • Loss of light reflex.
    • Reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy (most specific sign).
    • Purulent fluid behind TM (yellow/white).
    • Bullous myringitis — haemorrhagic bullae on TM (suggests Mycoplasma or influenza).

Complications

  • Tympanic membrane perforation — usually heals spontaneously; chronic perforation requires surgery (tympanoplasty).
  • Chronic suppurative otitis media — persistent ear discharge through perforation.
  • Cholesteatoma — squamous epithelial sac in middle ear; erodes bone; requires surgical excision.
  • Mastoiditis — infection spreads to mastoid air cells; pain, swelling behind ear; pinna pushed forward & downward; requires IV antibiotics ± mastoidectomy.
  • Labyrinthitis — vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, nystagmus.
  • Facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy — facial nerve passes through middle ear).
  • Intracranial — meningitis, brain abscess, subdural empyema, lateral sinus thrombosis, otitic hydrocephalus.
  • Hearing loss — conductive (usually transient); permanent sensorineural if inner ear involved.
  • Speech & language delay in recurrent AOM.

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • Clinical diagnosis — otoscopy; pneumatic otoscopy (reduced TM mobility); tympanometry (flat tympanogram = fluid).
  • Tympanocentesis — needle aspiration of middle ear fluid (rarely done; reserved for refractory, severe, immunocompromised, or neonatal AOM); culture & sensitivity.
  • Ear swab culture — if TM perforated with discharge.
  • Blood culture — in infants <12 weeks; if febrile & toxic.
  • CBG — leucocytosis.
  • CRP.
  • Audiometry — for hearing assessment after recovery; especially if recurrent.
  • Imaging:
    • CT temporal bone — if mastoiditis, cholesteatoma, intracranial complication suspected.
    • MRI brain — for intracranial extension.

Treatment

1. Symptomatic

  • Analgesia — paracetamol, ibuprofen; topical anaesthetic drops (benzocaine — not <2 yr in US).
  • Warm compress.
  • Decongestants (topical oxymetazoline) — controversial; may help Eustachian tube function; avoid prolonged use.
  • Antihistamines — if allergy component; not routinely for AOM.

2. Antibiotics — Decision to Treat

  • Observation (watchful waiting) — for children ≥2 yr with mild, unilateral AOM without severe symptoms; ensure follow-up in 48–72 h.
  • Antibiotics indicated:
    • Children <6 months — always treat.
    • Children 6 months–2 yr — bilateral AOM or severe symptoms (fever >39 °C, moderate-severe otalgia).
    • Children ≥2 yr — bilateral AOM with otorrhoea or severe symptoms.
    • Immunocompromised, chronic illness, craniofacial abnormality.
  • Drug of choice — Amoxicillin 45 mg/kg/day (high dose) BD × 5–10 days (<2 yr: 10 days; ≥2 yr: 5–7 days).
  • Alternative — Amoxicillin-clavulanate 90 mg/kg/day (if failure in 48–72 h, recent antibiotic use, conjunctivitis [likely H. influenzae β-lactamase producer]).
  • Penicillin allergy — Cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime (if non-type I hypersensitivity); Azithromycin, clarithromycin (if type I — but macrolide resistance in S. pneumoniae ~30%).
  • Treatment failure at 48–72 h — switch to amoxicillin-clavulanate; consider IM ceftriaxone × 3 days.
  • TM perforation with discharge — topical antibiotic drops (ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone) ± oral.

3. Surgical

  • Myringotomy — surgical incision of TM; for severe pain, refractory infection, mastoiditis.
  • Tympanostomy tube (grommet) — for recurrent AOM (≥3 episodes in 6 months, ≥4 in 12 months); chronic otitis media with effusion (>3 months with hearing loss).
  • Adenoidectomy — if adenoid hypertrophy contributes.
  • Mastoidectomy — for mastoiditis, cholesteatoma.

Prevention

  • Breastfeeding — at least 6 months; reduces AOM risk.
  • Avoid bottle feeding in supine position.
  • Avoid tobacco smoke exposure.
  • Reduce day care exposure (if possible).
  • Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) — reduces S. pneumoniae AOM.
  • Hib conjugate vaccine — reduces H. influenzae type b (but most AOM caused by non-typeable strains — limited benefit).
  • Influenza vaccine — annual; reduces influenza-related AOM.
  • Prophylactic antibiotics — amoxicillin or sulfisoxazole daily during winter; for recurrent AOM (limited use due to resistance).
  • Xylitol gum/lozenges — modest benefit.

Clinical Pearl

Pneumatic otoscopy is the most specific clinical sign of AOM — reduced mobility of tympanic membrane on insufflation indicates middle ear fluid. Most AOM in older children is viral or self-limited — observation without antibiotics is acceptable for mild cases (watchful waiting); ensure follow-up in 48–72 h. Amoxicillin (high dose — 90 mg/kg/day) remains first-line — despite pneumococcal resistance (15–35%), high-dose amoxicillin overcomes MIC; switch to amoxicillin-clavulanate if treatment failure or recent antibiotic exposure. Watch for mastoiditis — postauricular pain, swelling, erythema, protruding ear; requires IV antibiotics ± mastoidectomy. Always assess hearing after recurrent AOM — conductive hearing loss from persistent effusion may delay speech & language development; tympanostomy tubes if effusion >3 months with hearing loss. PCV13 vaccination has reduced pneumococcal AOM by ~30% — but serotype replacement (especially 19A, 6A) continues. Distinguish from otitis externa — pain on moving tragus, normal TM, normal middle ear; often Pseudomonas (swimmer's ear); topical antibiotics. India — AOM remains common; Hib vaccine (in pentavalent) & PCV13 (in UIP) reduce incidence; antibiotic stewardship important — avoid unnecessary antibiotics for viral URI.

Introduction

Mycetoma is a chronic subcutaneous infection with triad of tumefaction, sinus tracts, & discharge of grains. Based on causative organism, classified as eumycetoma (fungal) or actinomycetoma (bacterial — actinomycetes). Differentiation is critical because treatment differs dramatically.

Comparison

Feature Eumycetoma (Fungal) Actinomycetoma (Bacterial)
Causative organismTrue fungi — Madurella mycetomatis, M. grisea, Exophiala, Leptosphaeria, Pseudallescheria boydii, Acremonium, Fusarium, AspergillusFilamentous bacteria (actinomycetes) — Nocardia brasiliensis, N. asteroides, Streptomyces somaliensis, Actinomadura madurae, A. pelletieri
Frequency~40% of mycetoma cases~60% of cases
Grain colourOften black (Madurella, Exophiala) or white (Pseudallescheria, Acremonium, Fusarium)White or yellow (Nocardia, Actinomadura madurae); red (A. pelletieri); yellow-brown (Streptomyces somaliensis)
Grain sizeVariable (200–900 µm); largerSmaller (100–300 µm); more uniform
Hyphae morphology (KOH mount)Septate hyphae, 3–5 µm diameter; with chlamydospores; embedded in brown cement-like matrixFine filaments, 1 µm diameter (narrower than fungal hyphae); branching
Gram stainGram-positive broader hyphaeGram-positive branching filaments (beaded appearance)
Modified acid-fast stainNegativeWeakly acid-fast (Nocardia — partially retains carbol fuchsin with weak decolouriser)
GeographyAfrica (Sudan), India, Middle EastMexico, Central/South America; Africa; India
CultureSDA — grows slowly (4–6 weeks) at 25–30 °C; no cycloheximide (inhibits some fungi)SDA, BHI, blood agar, LJ — aerobic; grows in 2–4 weeks at 37 °C; chalky, powdery colonies
Bone involvementCommon; slowCommon; rapid
LesionWell-circumscribed; slower progressionMore inflammatory; faster progression
SerologyELISA, immunodiffusion for antibodies (Madurella)Limited availability
TreatmentAntifungals — itraconazole 200–400 mg/day for 6–12 months (or longer); terbinafine, voriconazole, posaconazole; amphotericin B for severe; surgical excision; amputation in advancedAntibiotics (Welsh regimen) — Streptomycin 1 g IM daily × 4 weeks + co-trimoxazole 960 mg BD × 12 months; add amikacin for refractory; dapsone, minocycline; surgical excision for localised
Response to treatmentPoor — cure rate 25–35%; high recurrenceGood — cure rate 60–90%
MortalityLow (chronic, but disabling)Low

Pathology

  • Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon — eosinophilic amorphous material (immune complex) surrounding grains; seen in both but more prominent in eumycetoma.
  • Granulomatous inflammation — epithelioid cells, giant cells, neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells.
  • Grain structure:
    • Eumycetoma — septate hyphae in matrix (PAS, GMS positive).
    • Actinomycetoma — fine filaments (Gram-positive; weakly acid-fast; GMS positive).

Clinical Pearl

The grain colour is the most useful bedside clue — black grains suggest eumycetoma (Madurella); white/yellow/red grains suggest actinomycetoma. KOH mount of grains distinguishes: eumycetoma — broad septate hyphae (3–5 µm); actinomycetoma — fine filaments (1 µm, weakly acid-fast — modified ZN). Actinomycetoma responds dramatically to antibiotics (Welsh regimen — streptomycin + co-trimoxazole, cure 60–90%) whereas eumycetoma requires long-term antifungals (itraconazole ± surgery, cure 25–35%). Always culture to confirm organism & type — empirical therapy without culture is unwise. Distinguish from actinomycosis — actinomycosis (Actinomyces israelii) is endogenous (oral flora), discharges sulphur granules (bacterial aggregates), responds to penicillin; mycetoma is exogenous (soil), discharges true fungal/bacterial grains, does not respond to penicillin. WHO declared mycetoma a Neglected Tropical Disease in 2016 — reflects recognition of burden in "mycetoma belt" (Sudan, India, Mexico). The "dot-in-circle" sign on MRI is highly specific — small hypointense foci (grains) within larger lesions.

Clinical Identification

The 10-year-old boy with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) presenting with severe pain, swelling, and likely black necrotic lesion around eye/nose/sinus — classic for rhinocerebral mucormycosis, a medical emergency. DKA is the most important risk factor because acidosis and high iron (free iron in acidosis) promote Mucorales growth.

Definition

Mucormycosis (zygomycosis) is an aggressive angioinvasive fungal infection caused by moulds of order Mucorales — most commonly Rhizopus arrhizus (oryzae), Mucor spp., Absidia (Lichtheimia), Apophysomyces, Saksenaea, Cunninghamella. Ubiquitous in environment (soil, decaying organic matter, bread mould).

Risk Factors

  • Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) — most important; acidosis dissociates iron from transferrin → free iron promotes Mucorales growth (no siderophore needed); acidosis also impairs neutrophil function.
  • Diabetes mellitus (even without DKA).
  • Haematological malignancy (AML, ALL) & neutropenia.
  • Stem cell or solid organ transplant.
  • Prolonged corticosteroid use (especially COVID-19 — "CAM" — COVID-associated mucormycosis).
  • Burns, trauma.
  • Iron overload — deferoxamine therapy (chelated iron used as siderophore by Mucorales); haemochromatosis.
  • IV drug use (cerebral mucormycosis).
  • Premature neonates (GI mucormycosis).
  • Malnutrition, HIV (less common than for aspergillosis).

Clinical Syndromes

1. Rhinocerebral Mucormycosis — Most Common (30–50%)

  • Most common in DKA.
  • Entry — inhalation of spores into nasal cavity → invade nasal mucosa & sinus → spread to orbit, brain (through cribriform plate / orbital apex).
  • Features:
    • Nasal stuffiness, blood-tinged nasal discharge, black necrotic eschar on nasal turbinate/palate (pathognomonic).
    • Facial pain, swelling, periorbital cellulitis.
    • Headache, fever.
    • Cranial nerve palsy (II, III, IV, V, VI) — blindness, ophthalmoplegia.
    • Black necrotic lesion on hard palate.
    • Acute angle-closure glaucoma (rare).
    • Cerebral involvement — altered sensorium, seizures, stroke (cavernous sinus thrombosis, internal carotid artery occlusion).
  • Rapidly progressive; fatal within days if untreated.

2. Pulmonary Mucormycosis

  • Seen in neutropenia, haematologic malignancy, transplant.
  • Features — fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis; rapidly progressive pneumonia.
  • Imaging — CT: nodules, consolidation, cavitation, halo sign, reverse halo sign (atoll sign); angioinvasion → pulmonary infarct.
  • High mortality (50–80%).

3. Cutaneous Mucormycosis

  • Entry — traumatic inoculation (burns, wounds, IV catheter sites, surgery, trauma).
  • Features — cellulitis, erythema, induration, rapidly progressive necrotic eschar; may disseminate.
  • Most treatable form if localised — surgical debridement + amphotericin B.

4. Gastrointestinal Mucormycosis (Rare)

  • Seen in neonates, malnutrition, extreme prematurity.
  • Stomach, colon, ileum — ulceration, necrosis, perforation, bleeding.
  • High mortality.

5. Disseminated Mucormycosis

  • Haematogenous spread — brain (most common); also liver, spleen, kidney, heart, skin.
  • Mortality ~95%.

6. Miscellaneous

  • Cerebral (isolated) — IV drug use; haematogenous.
  • Renal — isolated renal mucormycosis; IV drug use, diabetes.
  • Endocarditis, osteomyelitis, peritonitis (peritoneal dialysis).

Pathogenesis

  • Entry — inhalation (sinus/lung), ingestion (GI), or traumatic inoculation (skin).
  • Angioinvasion — hyphae invade blood vessels (especially arteries) → thrombosis, infarction, necrosis; haematogenous dissemination.
  • Virulence factors:
    • Iron acquisition — uses free iron in acidosis; deferoxamine (chelator) used as siderophore.
    • CotH ligand — binds GRP78 on endothelial cells; mediates invasion.
    • Thermotolerance — grows at 37 °C.
    • Spore coating — survives macrophage killing.
  • Host defences — macrophages (ingest spores); neutrophils (kill hyphae). Defective in neutropenia, DKA, steroid therapy.

Diagnosis

1. Specimen

  • Nasal turbinate / sinus biopsy / tissue — for rhinocerebral.
  • BAL, lung biopsy — for pulmonary.
  • Skin biopsy — for cutaneous.
  • CSF — rarely positive in cerebral.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • KOH mount / Calcofluor white:
    • Broad (6–15 µm), ribbon-like, aseptate (or pauciseptate) hyphae with right-angle (90°) branching; characteristic.
    • Contrast with Aspergillus — narrow (3–6 µm), septate, acute-angle (45°) branching.
  • Histopathology (GMS, PAS stain):
    • Broad aseptate hyphae invading tissue & blood vessels.
    • Angioinvasion with thrombosis & infarction.
    • Necrosis; sparse inflammatory response (especially in neutropenia).

3. Culture

  • Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) — without cycloheximide (inhibits Mucorales).
  • Incubate at 25–30 °C for 2–5 days (rapid growth).
  • Colony morphology:
    • Rhizopus — cottony, white to grey-brown to black ("bread mould").
    • Mucor — cottony, yellow-brown.
    • Absidia — similar.
  • Microscopy:
    • Rhizopus — sporangiophores arise from nodal rhizoids (root-like structures); sporangium terminal (round, filled with sporangiospores); no apophysis.
    • Mucor — no rhizoids; sporangiophores branch.
    • Absidia — rhizoids between sporangiophores (internodal); apophysis present.
  • Culture may be negative despite tissue invasion; diagnosis often rests on histopathology.

4. Other Tests

  • No reliable antigen test — galactomannan & β-D-glucan are NEGATIVE in mucormycosis (distinguishes from aspergillosis).
  • PCR — investigational; Mucorales-specific PCR on tissue, blood; useful in research.
  • Imaging:
    • CT sinus — sinus opacification, bony erosion, orbital extension, intracranial extension.
    • CT chest — nodules, consolidation, halo sign, reverse halo sign (atoll).
    • MRI brain — cavernous sinus thrombosis, cerebral infarct, abscess.
  • CBG — may show neutropenia, ketoacidosis.
  • Blood glucose, ketones, ABG — for DKA.

Treatment — Emergency!

  • Reverse underlying condition — correct DKA (insulin, fluids, electrolytes); reduce immunosuppression; G-CSF for neutropenia; stop deferoxamine.
  • Surgical debridement — extensive & repeated; remove all necrotic tissue; may require orbital exenteration, palatectomy, sinus clearance; life-saving in rhinocerebral.
  • Antifungal:
    • Liposomal amphotericin B 5–10 mg/kg/day IV — drug of choice; high dose; continue until clinical stabilisation & negative follow-up imaging (typically 4–6 weeks minimum).
    • Posaconazole IV/PO — step-down therapy after amphotericin; salvage.
    • Isavuconazole IV/PO — alternative; approved for mucormycosis.
    • Combination — amphotericin + echinocandin (caspofungin) — controversial.
  • Hyperbaric oxygen therapy — adjunct; controversial; may help wound healing.
  • Salvage therapy — iron chelation (deferasirox — controversial; FIRST trial showed harm); high-dose amphotericin + caspofungin.
  • Mortality — 30–50% rhinocerebral; 50–80% pulmonary; >95% disseminated.

Prevention

  • Strict glucose control in diabetics; prevent DKA.
  • Reduce immunosuppression when possible.
  • Avoid deferoxamine in iron overload — use deferasirox instead.
  • HEPA-filtered rooms for high-risk patients.
  • Antifungal prophylaxis — posaconazole in neutropenia / transplant; covers Aspergillus + Mucorales.
  • Avoid construction dust / gardening for high-risk patients.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important bedside clue is a black necrotic eschar on nasal turbinate or hard palate in a patient with DKA — consider rhinocerebral mucormycosis a medical emergency; start liposomal amphotericin B & arrange surgical debridement within hours. The histopathology is pathognomonic — broad (6–15 µm), ribbon-like, aseptate hyphae with right-angle (90°) branching, angioinvasive; contrast with Aspergillus (narrow septate acute-angle branching). Galactomannan & β-D-glucan are NEGATIVE in mucormycosis — if positive, suggests aspergillosis; if negative in high-risk patient, still suspect mucormycosis. Treatment requires aggressive surgical debridement + high-dose liposomal amphotericin B (5–10 mg/kg/day) — voriconazole is INEFFECTIVE (Mucorales resistant); this is why distinguishing from aspergillosis is critical. The COVID-19 pandemic caused an epidemic of COVID-associated mucormycosis (CAM) in India (2021) — uncontrolled diabetes + steroid therapy + possibly zinc/iron supplementation created perfect storm; >40,000 cases & thousands of deaths. Correct DKA aggressively — free iron in acidosis promotes Mucorales growth; insulin, hydration, electrolyte correction. Always check for orbital/cerebral extension — cranial nerve palsy, vision loss, altered sensorium indicate advanced disease & poor prognosis. Repeat debridement often necessary — infection spreads rapidly along vessels; "one debridement is rarely enough".

Introduction

Measles (Rubeola) is a highly contagious acute viral exanthem caused by measles virus (Paramyxoviridae, Morbillivirus). Characterised by prodrome (fever, 3 Cs — cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots, & characteristic cephalocaudal spread of maculopapular rash.

Clinical Stages

1. Incubation Period (8–12 days)

  • Asymptomatic; patient not infectious until end of incubation.
  • Virus replicates in respiratory epithelium & lymphoid tissue; primary & secondary viraemia.

2. Prodromal Stage (3–5 days)

  • Fever — gradually rising, may reach 39–40 °C.
  • 3 Cs:
    • Cough — dry, brassy, persistent (laryngotracheitis).
    • Coryza — profuse nasal discharge, sneezing.
    • Conjunctivitis — bilateral, with photophobia, lacrimation, exudate; swollen eyelids.
  • Malaise, anorexia, fatigue, irritability.
  • Myalgia, headache.
  • Koplik spots — pathognomonic; appear 1–2 days before rash.
    • Grayish-white papules (1–3 mm) on erythematous base.
    • Located on buccal mucosa opposite lower molars.
    • Look like "grains of salt on a red background".
    • Disappear after rash appears.
  • High infectivity during prodrome (virus shedding in respiratory secretions).

3. Rash Stage (Day 14; lasts 5–7 days)

  • Maculopapular, erythematous, blanching rash.
  • Cephalocaudal spread:
    • Day 1 — appears behind ears & on face/hairline; spreads to neck, upper trunk.
    • Day 2 — spreads to trunk, arms.
    • Day 3 — reaches legs, feet, palms & soles.
    • Lesions may coalesce, especially on face & upper body.
  • Rash becomes non-blanching & brownish by day 4–5 (capillary leakage); may have petechiae.
  • Fever peaks as rash appears; fever defervesces over 1–2 days after rash peaks.
  • Fine desquamation (peeling) — not as prominent as scarlet fever.
  • Rash fades in same order (face first to clear).

4. Recovery Stage

  • Symptoms improve after rash peaks; cough may persist 1–2 weeks.
  • Patient remains infectious until 4 days after rash onset.
  • Brownish hyperpigmentation of skin (especially in dark-skinned patients); lasts weeks.

Other Clinical Features

  • Lymphadenopathy — generalised; cervical & suboccipital.
  • Splenomegaly.
  • GI symptoms — diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain; dehydration.
  • Conjunctivitis — severe, with photophobia; corneal ulceration in vitamin A deficiency.
  • Otitis media — most common complication (5–15%).
  • Pneumonia — viral (giant cell pneumonia) or secondary bacterial (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, S. aureus).
  • Encephalitis — ~1 in 1000; ADEM (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis).
  • SSPE — subacute sclerosing panencephalitis; rare; 5–15 years after measles; progressive fatal neurodegenerative disease.
  • Immunosuppression — lasts weeks-months; predisposes to secondary infections; tuberculin test becomes negative ("measles anergy").

Atypical Measles Syndrome

  • Seen in individuals who received killed measles vaccine (1963–67) & subsequently exposed to wild virus.
  • Features — high fever, headache, abdominal pain; atypical rash — petechial, vesicular, urticarial; starts on extremities (palms & soles) & spreads centrally (opposite of typical measles).
  • Severe pneumonia with pleural effusion, hilar lymphadenopathy.
  • Now rare — killed vaccine discontinued.

Modified Measles

  • In individuals with partial immunity (passive antibody from IG, prior vaccination with waning immunity).
  • Milder prodrome, fewer Koplik spots, sparse rash; shorter course.
  • Less infectious.

Clinical Pearl

Koplik spots are the pathognomonic clinical sign of measles — grayish-white papules on erythematous buccal mucosa opposite lower molars; appear 1–2 days before rash; allow diagnosis during prodrome before rash appears. The classic cephalocaudal rash spread — face/hairline → trunk → extremities → palms/soles — is characteristic; rash on palms & soles is highly suggestive of measles (also syphilis, RMSF, hand-foot-mouth, Kawasaki, meningococcaemia). The 3 Cs of prodrome — cough, coryza, conjunctivitis — with fever should raise suspicion even before rash. Measles causes profound immunosuppression lasting weeks-months — basis for secondary bacterial pneumonia (most common cause of death), otitis media, diarrhoea, reactivation of TB; tuberculin test becomes temporarily negative — re-test 4–6 weeks after recovery. Vitamin A supplementation is the only evidence-based treatment that reduces mortality — WHO recommends for all children with measles (50,000 IU if <6 mo; 100,000 IU if 6–12 mo; 200,000 IU if >12 mo; 2 doses 24 h apart; third dose 4 weeks later if xerophthalmia). SSPE — rare late complication; 5–15 years after measles; behavioural changes → myoclonic seizures → dementia → death within 1–3 years; measles antibody in CSF diagnostic. Measles is the most contagious human virus (R₀ 12–18); herd immunity requires ≥95% coverage; even small dips below this lead to outbreaks (2019 Samoa outbreak — 87 deaths). Distinguish from rubella — milder prodrome, no Koplik spots, postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy, shorter rash; congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) is the main concern.

Clinical Identification

The patient with multiple, symmetrical, hypopigmented skin lesions — especially if associated with sensory loss, nerve thickening, or family history — is most consistent with Leprosy (Hansen's disease), specifically Borderline Lepromatous (BL) or Lepromatous (LL) leprosy given the multiple, symmetrical distribution.

Definition

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae (or M. lepromatosis) — affects skin & peripheral nerves. Clinical presentation depends on host cell-mediated immunity — strong CMI → tuberculoid (paucibacillary); weak CMI → lepromatous (multibacillary).

Clinical Spectrum (Ridley-Jopling)

Type Lesions Sensation Nerves Smear
Indeterminate (I)Single hypopigmented macule; vagueNormal/minimal lossNot thickenedNegative
Tuberculoid (TT)Single/few well-defined anaesthetic hypopigmented plaque with raised edges; dry, hairlessMarked lossOne nerve thickened (great auricular, ulnar, peroneal)Negative/scanty
Borderline Tuberculoid (BT)Multiple asymmetric plaques with satellite lesionsLossMultiple nervesScanty
Borderline (BB)Multiple annular lesions with punched-out centresLossMultipleModerate
Borderline Lepromatous (BL)Numerous bilateral lesions; nodules, plaques, maculesVariableMultiple; glove-stocking anaesthesiaHigh
Lepromatous (LL)Diffuse infiltration; nodules, plaques; leonine facies; madarosis (eyebrow alopecia); saddle nose; multiple symmetrical lesionsSymmetric, widespread loss (glove-stocking)Symmetric thickening; glove-stocking anaesthesiaVery high (globi)

WHO Operational Classification

  • Paucibacillary (PB) — 1–5 lesions; smear-negative; treated with PB-MDT (rifampicin + dapsone) × 6 months.
  • Multibacillary (MB) — >5 lesions or smear-positive; treated with MB-MDT (rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone) × 12 months.

Clinical Features — Hypopigmented Lesions

  • Hypopigmentation (not depigmentation) — partial loss of pigment (vitiligo is depigmentation — complete loss).
  • Erythema — lesions may be erythematous or copper-coloured.
  • Anaesthesia — most reliable sign; test with cotton wisp (light touch) & pinprick (pain); temperature sensation also lost.
  • Anhidrosis — lesions do not sweat (dry).
  • Hair loss — lesions hairless (especially TT).
  • Thickness — TT lesions raised (plaque); LL lesions infiltrated (nodules, diffuse thickening).
  • Distribution:
    • TT/BT — asymmetric, few lesions.
    • BL/LL — symmetric, multiple, widespread; face (leonine facies — forehead, eyebrows, ears, nose), trunk, extremities.

Neurological Involvement

  • Skin lesions anaesthetic — earliest & most reliable sign.
  • Peripheral nerve thickening:
    • Great auricular (neck — visible crossing sternocleidomastoid).
    • Ulnar (above elbow — cubital tunnel; palpable).
    • Radial cutaneous (wrist).
    • Common peroneal (knee — fibular neck; foot drop).
    • Posterior tibial (behind medial malleolus).
    • Facial (upper trunk — lagophthalmos, corneal anaesthesia).
  • Claw hand (ulnar nerve — 4th & 5th digits flexion).
  • Foot drop (peroneal nerve — inability to dorsiflex foot).
  • Claw toes (posterior tibial nerve).
  • Lagophthalmos, corneal anaesthesia, exposure keratitis (facial nerve).
  • Trophic ulcers — painless plantar ulcers; autoamputation of digits due to repeated trauma & infection.

Reactions

  • Type 1 (Reversal reaction):
    • Delayed Type IV hypersensitivity; affects borderline (BT, BB, BL) leprosy.

  • Type 2 (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum — ENL):
    • Immune complex (Type III) reaction; affects LL & BL.
    • Crops of painful erythematous nodules on face, extensor surfaces; fever, malaise, iritis, orchitis, neuritis, dactylitis, lymphadenitis, glomerulonephritis.

  • WHO cardinal signs (≥1 confirms leprosy):
    1. Hypopigmented/reddish skin lesion with definite loss of sensation.
    2. Thickened peripheral nerves with loss of sensation in area supplied.
    3. Skin smear positive for AFB.
  • Skin slit-smear — Ziehl-Neelsen or Fite-Faraco stain; from ear lobes & lesion edges; Bacterial Index (BI, Ridley 0–6+).
  • Skin biopsy — histopathology; Fite-Faraco stain; classify type.
  • Nerve biopsy — sural nerve for pure neuritic leprosy.
  • Serology — PGL-1 IgM ELISA; useful for MB but not PB.
  • PCR — M. leprae DNA (RLEP target); for PB & difficult cases.

  • Vitiligo — depigmentation (complete loss); normal sensation; autoimmune.
  • Pityriasis versicolor — Malassezia; fine scale; KOH positive; normal sensation.
  • Pityriasis alba — post-inflammatory hypopigmentation in atopic children; normal sensation.
  • Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) — nodules/macules on face; history of kala-azar; biopsy shows Leishman-Donovan bodies.
  • Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor — fungal; KOH shows hyphae & spores ("spaghetti & meatballs").
  • Tuberculoid leprosy — single/few lesions with anaesthesia.
  • Syphilis (secondary) — maculopapular rash including palms/soles; serology positive.

The single most reliable clinical sign of leprosy is anaesthetic skin lesion — test sensation with cotton wisp & pinprick; a hypopigmented or reddish patch that does not feel touch/pin = leprosy until proven otherwise. Symmetrical multiple hypopigmented lesions suggest BL/LL (multibacillary); asymmetric single/few lesions with marked anaesthesia suggest TT/BT (paucibacillary). Always examine peripheral nerves — great auricular, ulnar, peroneal, posterior tibial — for thickening & tenderness; pure neuritic leprosy (no skin lesions) is common in India & requires nerve biopsy. Skin smear from ear lobe & lesion edge (ZN or Fite-Faraco) shows AFB in multibacillary cases. Biopsy with Fite-Faraco stain confirms & classifies disease even in paucibacillary cases. PCR for M. leprae (RLEP target) is useful for paucibacillary & pure neuritic leprosy. Always look for & treat reactions (Type 1 reversal & Type 2 ENL) — these can cause irreversible nerve damage if untreated; thalidomide for ENL is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy (severe phocomelia). India eliminated leprosy as public health problem in 2005 (prevalence <1/10,000) but still has ~120,000 new cases annually; hidden cases (untreated, marginalised) are the major challenge. Distinguish from vitiligo — vitiligo is depigmentation (complete loss, chalk-white) with normal sensation; leprosy is hypopigmentation (partial loss) with anaesthesia.

Introduction

Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — small (55 nm), non-enveloped, double-stranded circular DNA virus of family Papillomaviridae — infects squamous epithelium (skin & mucosa). More than 200 genotypes identified; classified by tropism (cutaneous vs mucosal) & oncogenic risk (low-risk vs high-risk). Transmission — skin-to-skin contact, sexual, vertical.

Two Examples of HPV Infections

1. Cutaneous Warts (Verrucae) — Low-Risk HPV Types

  • Common wart (Verruca vulgaris):
    • Cause — HPV-2, 4, 27, 57 (most common: HPV-2).
    • Site — fingers, hands, knees (trauma-prone areas).
    • Clinical — rough, hyperkeratotic, firm papules (1–10 mm); may have black dots (thrombosed capillaries); single or multiple.
    • Usually self-limiting (resolve in 1–2 years); may persist.
    • Treatment — topical salicylic acid, cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen), electrocautery, laser, cantharidin, imiquimod.
  • Plantar wart (Verruca plantaris):
    • Cause — HPV-1 (deep, painful myrmecia), HPV-2, 4, 27, 57.
    • Site — soles (pressure points); endophytic due to pressure.
    • Clinical — thickened, hyperkeratotic plaque with black dots; pain on walking (like stepping on pebble).
  • Flat wart (Verruca plana):
    • Cause — HPV-3, 10, 28.
    • Site — face, hands, shins (especially children).
    • Clinical — smooth, flat-topped, flesh-coloured papules (1–5 mm); multiple; linear arrangement (Koebner phenomenon).
  • Butcher's wart:
    • Cause — HPV-2, 7.
    • Seen in meat/fish handlers; large cauliflower-like warts on hands.
  • Epidermodysplasia verruciformis:
    • Rare genetic disorder (EVER1/EVER2 mutations); impaired cell-mediated immunity to HPV.
    • Disseminated flat warts & macules from childhood; HPV-5, 8 (high-risk for skin cancer).
    • 50% develop squamous cell carcinoma in sun-exposed areas.

2. Anogenital Warts (Condylomata Acuminata) — Low-Risk Mucosal HPV

  • Cause — HPV-6, 11 (low-risk; 90% of genital warts).
  • Transmission — sexual contact (most common STI); also vertical (during birth → juvenile recurrent respiratory papillomatosis).
  • Sites — vulva, vagina, cervix, penis (glans, prepuce, shaft), perianal area, urethra, anus; oropharynx.
  • Clinical:
    • Soft, fleshy, cauliflower-like (verrucous) growths; pink, flesh-coloured, or hyperpigmented.
    • Single or multiple; may coalesce into large masses.
    • Usually painless; may cause itching, burning, bleeding, dyspareunia.
    • Incubation — 1–8 months (average 3 months).
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical appearance.
    • Acetowhite test — 5% acetic acid turns lesions white (sensitivity high, specificity low).
    • Colposcopy — for cervical lesions.
    • Biopsy — if atypical, ulcerated, or refractory; rule out malignancy.
    • PCR — genotyping (high-risk vs low-risk).
  • Treatment:
    • Patient-applied — Imiquimod 5% cream; Podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution/gel; Sinecatechins (green tea extract) 15% ointment.
    • Provider-administered — Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen); Podophyllin resin 10–25%; Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) 80–90%; Surgical excision; Electrocautery; Laser (CO₂).
    • May resolve spontaneously (10–30% in 3 months).

Other HPV Infections (brief)

3. Cervical Cancer & Other Cancers — High-Risk HPV

  • Cause — HPV-16, 18 (cause 70% of cervical cancers); also 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68.
  • Mechanism — E6 protein degrades p53 (tumour suppressor); E7 inactivates Rb; E5 activates EGFR. Persistent infection → CIN (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia) → invasive cancer over 10–30 years.
  • Other cancers — anal, oropharyngeal (base of tongue, tonsil), penile, vulvar, vaginal.
  • Screening — Pap smear (cytology); HPV DNA testing (co-testing ≥30 yr); colposcopy for abnormal cytology.
  • Treatment — CIN 1 (observe); CIN 2/3 (LEEP, cone biopsy, cryotherapy); invasive cancer (surgery + chemo-radiation).

4. Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis

  • Cause — HPV-6, 11 (vertical transmission at birth).
  • Site — larynx, vocal cords; rarely trachea, bronchi, lungs.
  • Clinical — hoarseness, stridor, respiratory obstruction; recurrent despite surgery; may require tracheostomy.
  • Treatment — laser excision, microdebrider; adjuvant cidofovir, interferon, bevacizumab; HPV vaccine as adjuvant.
  • May rarely progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

5. Conjunctival Papilloma

  • Cause — HPV-6, 11.
  • Benign vascular lesion of conjunctiva; surgical excision; recurrence common.

HPV Vaccination

  • Gardasil 9 (9-valent) — covers HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58.
  • Cervarix (bivalent) — HPV 16, 18.
  • Gardasil (quadrivalent) — HPV 6, 11, 16, 18.
  • Schedule — 2 doses if <15 yr (0, 6–12 months); 3 doses if ≥15 yr (0, 2, 6 months).
  • Recommended — boys & girls aged 9–14 years; gender-neutral vaccination now recommended.
  • India's CERVAVAC — indigenously developed quadrivalent vaccine (Serum Institute of India); launched 2023.

Clinical Pearl

HPV vaccination is the most important preventive intervention against cervical cancer — the first anti-cancer vaccine. Gardasil 9 covers 90% of cervical cancer-causing types (16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58) + 90% of genital warts (6, 11). Recommended at ages 9–14 years before sexual debut — 2-dose schedule if <15 years; 3 doses if ≥15 years. Gender-neutral vaccination now recommended — prevents anal, oropharyngeal, penile cancers in males. Pap smear screening — every 3 years for women 21–65; or HPV DNA testing every 5 years for women 25–65; co-testing (Pap + HPV) every 5 years for 30–65. HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer — rising dramatically in men (Western countries); presents in younger non-smokers; better prognosis than HPV-negative (smoking/alcohol-related) oropharyngeal cancer. India has high cervical cancer burden (~75,000 deaths/year — second most common cancer in women); CERVAVAC (indigenous quadrivalent vaccine, ~₹200/dose for public sector) launched 2023 — major step toward elimination. WHO aims to eliminate cervical cancer (<4/100,000) by 2120 — requires 90% vaccination, 70% screening, 90% treatment access.

Introduction

Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) — also called atypical mycobacteria, mycobacteria other than tuberculosis (MOTT) — are environmental mycobacteria (found in water, soil, dust) that cause opportunistic infections in humans. They are NOT transmitted person-to-person (unlike M. tuberculosis). With improved survival of immunocompromised patients (HIV, transplant) & better diagnostic techniques, NTM infections are increasing.

Classification — Runyon Classification (1959)

Based on growth rate, pigment production, & colony morphology:

Group Characteristic Examples
Group I — PhotochromogensProduce pigment only on exposure to light (yellow-orange); slow grower (>7 days)M. kansasii, M. marinum, M. simiae, M. asiaticum
Group II — ScotochromogensProduce pigment in dark & light (yellow-orange); slow growerM. scrofulaceum, M. gordonae (tap water — common contaminant), M. szulgai, M. xenopi
Group III — Non-chromogensNo pigment; slow growerM. avium-intracellulare complex (MAC), M. ulcerans (Buruli ulcer), M. malmoense, M. haemophilum, M. gastri
Group IV — Rapid growersGrow in <7 days; no pigment (or variable)M. fortuitum, M. chelonae, M. abscessus, M. smegmatis (non-pathogenic commensal)

Two Examples — Detailed

1. Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare Complex (MAC / MAI)

  • Non-chromogen; slow grower (10–21 days); non-pigmented colonies on LJ.
  • Habitat — water, soil, birds, animals.
  • Transmission — inhalation (aerosolised water), ingestion (contaminated food/water); NOT person-to-person.
  • Clinical syndromes:
    • Disseminated MAC — in advanced HIV (CD4 <50); fever, weight loss, night sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, anaemia, diarrhoea; bacteraemia.
    • Pulmonary MAC — chronic cough, sputum, weight loss; in older women with bronchiectasis (Lady Windermere syndrome — middle lobe), elderly men with COPD, cystic fibrosis patients.
    • Cervical lymphadenitis — children 1–5 yr; unilateral painless node; surgical excision curative.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Sputum / blood culture — BACTEC MGIT (positive in 7–14 days).
    • Colonies — thin, translucent, smooth (or rough).
    • Biochemical — negative for niacin, nitrate; positive for tellurite reduction; urease variable; heat-stable catalase positive; tween hydrolysis negative.
    • PCR — MAC-specific targets (DT1, IS1245, IS1311).
    • HPLC — mycolic acid pattern.
    • MALDI-TOF — rapid identification.
  • Treatment:
    • Disseminated MAC (HIV) — clarithromycin/azithromycin + ethambutol ± rifabutin; prophylaxis with azithromycin 1200 mg weekly if CD4 <50.
    • Pulmonary MAC — rifampicin + ethambutol + macrolide (azithromycin/clarithromycin) for ≥12 months after culture conversion; amikacin in severe.
    • Lymphadenitis — surgical excision.

2. Mycobacterium kansasii

  • Photochromogen — yellow-orange pigment in light; slow grower (2–4 weeks).
  • Habitat — water (tap water); soil.
  • Clinical syndromes:
    • Pulmonary disease — resembles pulmonary TB; cavitary lesions in upper lobes; in middle-aged men with COPD, pneumoconiosis, smoking, alcoholism, HIV.
    • Disseminated disease — in HIV; bone, skin.
    • Cervical lymphadenitis — children.
    • Skin/soft tissue infection — trauma; localised.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Sputum culture — slow grower; photochromogenic.
    • Biochemical — positive nitrate reduction (distinguishes from M. tuberculosis); positive tween hydrolysis; negative niacin; heat-stable catalase positive.
    • PCR — ITS, 16S rRNA.
    • HPLC, MALDI-TOF.
  • Treatment:
    • Rifampicin + ethambutol + isoniazid (or macrolide) for 12–18 months.
    • More responsive to anti-TB drugs than other NTM.

Other Important NTM

3. Mycobacterium marinum — Photochromogen

  • Habitat — fresh & salt water (fish tanks, swimming pools, oceans).
  • Clinical — swimming pool granuloma / fish tank granuloma; reddish papule at site of trauma (finger, hand); may spread along lymphatics (sporotrichoid pattern); deepest infection — tenosynovitis, osteomyelitis.
  • Optimum growth — 30–32 °C (not 37 °C — explains cooler skin location).
  • Treatment — clarithromycin, minocycline, doxycycline, rifampicin + ethambutol; 3–4 months.

4. Mycobacterium ulcerans — Non-chromogen

  • Cause of Buruli ulcer — third most common mycobacterial disease after TB & leprosy.
  • Endemic — West Africa, Australia, Southeast Asia.
  • Clinical — painless ulcer with undermined edges; starts as painless nodule → ulcerates; extensive skin & soft tissue destruction; toxin (mycolactone) causes necrosis.
  • Treatment — rifampicin + clarithromycin (or fluoroquinolone) for 8 weeks; surgical debridement; skin grafting.

5. Mycobacterium fortuitum, M. chelonae, M. abscessus — Rapid Growers

  • Grow in <7 days; colonies on LJ or blood agar within 3–5 days.
  • Clinical syndromes:
    • Skin & soft tissue infection — post-traumatic, post-surgical (especially post-laparoscopy, post-cosmetic surgery, post-acupuncture, post-tattoo); abscesses, cellulitis, ulcers.
    • Catheter-related infection, post-injection abscesses.
    • Pulmonary disease (especially M. abscessus in cystic fibrosis).
    • Disseminated infection (immunocompromised).
  • Outbreaks — post-surgical wound infections (especially M. chelonae & M. abscessus); contaminated instruments, solutions.
  • Treatment:
    • M. fortuitum — amikacin + fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) + imipenem; oral ciprofloxacin + doxycycline.
    • M. chelonae — tobramycin + clarithromycin; surgical debridement.
    • M. abscessus — amikacin + cefoxitin/imipenem + clarithromycin; multiple drug resistance; surgical excision often required.

Distinguishing NTM from M. tuberculosis

Feature M. tuberculosis NTM
TransmissionAirborne person-to-personEnvironmental (water, soil); NOT person-to-person
PigmentNon-pigmented (buff)Variable — photochromogen, scotochromogen, non-chromogen
Growth rateSlow (2–8 weeks)Variable — slow (4–8 weeks) or rapid (<7 days)
Temperature37 °CVariable — M. marinum 30 °C; M. ulcerans 30 °C; M. xenopi 42 °C
Niacin testPositiveNegative (except M. simiae)
Nitrate reductionPositiveVariable (M. kansasii +; MAC –)
Catalase (heat-stable)Negative (lost at 68 °C)Positive
Tween hydrolysisPositive (5 days)Variable
PyrazinamidasePositiveNegative (most)
PathogenicityStrong — always pathogenicOpportunistic — requires host defect
TreatmentStandard ATT (HRZE)Species-specific; macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, often resistant to standard ATT

Clinical Pearl

NTM should be suspected when: (1) Acid-fast bacilli seen on sputum smear but patient does not respond to standard ATT; (2) AFB-positive smear in patient with no TB risk factors but environmental exposure (water tank, fish tank); (3) AFB in surgical wound after cosmetic surgery / laparoscopy; (4) Chronic cutaneous ulcer in immunocompromised; (5) Cervical lymphadenitis in child (M. scrofulaceum, MAC — surgical excision, not ATT). Always confirm NTM with culture — single positive sputum culture may be contamination (especially M. gordonae — tap water contaminant). ATS/IDSA criteria require ≥2 positive sputum cultures (or 1 positive BAL) + clinical & radiological features. M. abscessus is the most drug-resistant NTM — often requires prolonged IV amikacin + cefoxitin/imipenem + oral macrolide; surgical excision for localised disease; poor prognosis in cystic fibrosis. M. marinum — "fish tank granuloma"; ask about tropical fish hobby or swimming pool exposure; grows at 30 °C (not 37 °C) — incubate at lower temperature. India's National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) does not include NTM surveillance; NTM infections are likely underdiagnosed. Antibiotic resistance is common in NTM — always do susceptibility testing; empirical ATT (HRZE) is often ineffective.

Introduction

Several parasites can form cysts in human skeletal muscle, typically as part of their life cycle or as aberrant migration. The two most important are Taenia solium (Cysticercus cellulosae — cysticercosis) and Trichinella spiralis (trichinellosis).

Two Important Parasites Forming Cysts in Skeletal Muscle

1. Taenia solium — Cysticercus cellulosae (Cysticercosis)

  • Parasite — pork tapeworm; T. solium.
  • Life cycle:
    • Definitive host — human (adult tapeworm in small intestine → eggs in faeces).
    • Intermediate host — pig (cysticercus cellulosae in muscle); human (accidental intermediate — cysticercosis).
  • Transmission to humans (cysticercosis):
    • Ingestion of T. solium eggs from contaminated food/water (faecal-oral).
    • Autoinfection — reverse peristalsis brings gravid proglottids/eggs from intestine to stomach; or faecal-oral self-infection.
    • NOT from eating undercooked pork (that causes intestinal taeniasis, not cysticercosis).
  • Pathogenesis:
    1. Eggs hatch in stomach & upper small intestine → oncospheres (hexacanth embryos).
    2. Oncospheres penetrate intestinal wall → bloodstream → disseminate to brain, eye, muscle, subcutaneous tissue.
    3. Develop into cysticerci (cysticercus cellulosae) — fluid-filled cyst (5–20 mm) with invaginated scolex (has suckers & hooklets).
    4. Live cysts cause minimal inflammation (immune evasion).
    5. When cyst dies (after 2–5 years) → intense inflammatory reaction → symptoms (seizures in brain; painful nodules in muscle; visual loss in eye).
    6. Eventually calcifies.
  • Skeletal muscle involvement:
    • Common site — skeletal muscle (along with brain, eye, subcutaneous tissue).
    • Usually asymptomatic; may cause myalgia, weakness.
    • Calcified cysticerci — visible on X-ray as elliptical ("cigar-shaped") calcifications in muscle, oriented along long axis of muscle fibres; pathognomonic.
    • Subcutaneous nodules — palpable; rice-grain size; biopsy shows cysticercus.
  • Clinical features:
    • Neurocysticercosis (NCC) — most common manifestation; seizures, headache, raised ICP, focal deficits; leading cause of adult-onset epilepsy in endemic areas.
    • Ocular cysticercosis — visual loss, retinal detachment.
    • Muscle/subcutaneous — usually asymptomatic; calcified nodules.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical + imaging.
    • CT/MRI brain — cyst with scolex ("hole-with-dot" sign); calcified lesions.
    • X-ray soft tissue — "cigar-shaped" calcifications in muscle.
    • Serology — EITB (enzymatic immunotransfer blot) for T. solium antibodies; ELISA.
    • Biopsy of subcutaneous nodule — cysticercus cellulosae.
    • Stool examination — for T. solium eggs/proglottids (identifies tapeworm carrier — source).
  • Treatment:
    • Albendazole 15 mg/kg/day × 7–14 days OR Praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day × 15 days — kills viable cysts.
    • Corticosteroids (dexamethasone/prednisolone) — before & during antiparasitic therapy to prevent inflammatory response to dying cysts.
    • Anticonvulsants — for seizures.
    • Surgical — for ocular, spinal cysts; ventricular shunt for hydrocephalus.
    • Calcified cysts — no antiparasitic needed (dead); anticonvulsants only.

2. Trichinella spiralis — Trichinellosis (Trichinosis)

  • Parasite — nematode (roundworm); Trichinella spiralis; other species — T. nativa (arctic), T. britovi, T. pseudospiralis, T. nelsoni.
  • Life cycle:
    • All stages occur in a single host (no environmental stage).
    • Adult worms in small intestine (intracellular in epithelial cells); male 1.5 mm × 40 µm; female 3–4 mm × 60 µm.
    • Viviparous — female releases larvae (100 µm) into bloodstream; larvae disseminate.
    • Larvae encyst in skeletal muscle — preferentially diaphragm, extraocular muscles, masseter, tongue, intercostal muscles, pectoral, deltoid, biceps, gastrocnemius (muscles with high blood flow).
    • Larvae coil inside nurse cells (modified muscle cell); encyst within 4–6 weeks; calcify within 6–18 months; remain viable for years (10+ years).
    • When another animal eats the encysted larvae (e.g., pig eats rat; human eats undercooked pork), larvae mature into adults in the new host's intestine → cycle continues.
  • Transmission to humans:
    • Eating undercooked pork (most common).
    • Eating undercooked wild game — bear, boar, walrus, horse meat (T. nativa in arctic — resistant to freezing).
    • Horse meat — Europe outbreaks.
  • Incubation — 1–2 weeks (range 1–35 days).
  • Clinical phases:
    • Phase 1 — Intestinal (1–7 days): nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting; due to adult worms in intestine.
    • Phase 2 — Migration (1–2 weeks): fever, myalgia (especially extraocular, masseter, diaphragm), periorbital oedema (pathognomonic), headache, weakness; eosinophilia; allergic reactions (urticaria); myocarditis, pneumonitis, encephalitis (severe).
    • Phase 3 — Encystment (2–3 weeks): symptoms subside; larvae encyst in muscle; persistent myalgia, weakness; calcification over months-years.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical — triad of fever, periorbital oedema, myalgia; eosinophilia; history of undercooked pork/wild game.
    • Serology — ELISA, immunoblot for Trichinella antibodies; appears 2–3 weeks after infection.
    • Muscle biopsy — gold standard; press muscle tissue between 2 slides & examine under microscope for coiled larvae; or histopathology with H&E; larvae in nurse cells.
    • CBG — eosinophilia (10–70%); leucocytosis; raised CPK, LDH (muscle breakdown).
    • PCR — investigational.
    • Other — ECG (myocarditis), chest X-ray (pneumonitis).
  • Treatment:
    • Albendazole 400 mg BD × 8–14 days OR Mebendazole 200–400 mg TID × 3 days then 400 mg TID × 10 days — kills adult worms & larvae.
    • Corticosteroids (prednisolone 30–60 mg/day) — for severe symptoms, myocarditis, CNS involvement, allergic reactions; reduces inflammation from dying larvae.
    • Analgesics — NSAIDs for myalgia.
    • Supportive — fluids, antipyretics, cardiac monitoring.
  • Prevention:
    • Cook pork & wild game thoroughly (≥71 °C / 160 °F internal temperature).
    • Freeze pork <15 cm thick at –15 °C for 20 days (kills T. spiralis; NOT effective against T. nativa — arctic, freeze-resistant).
    • Avoid eating undercooked wild game (bear, walrus).
    • Proper pig husbandry — cook feed; rodent control.
    • Meat inspection in slaughterhouses.

Other Parasites That Can Form Cysts/Encyst in Muscle (Less Common)

  • Echinococcus granulosus — hydatid cyst; rare in muscle (liver 60%, lung 20%); when in muscle — slowly growing cyst; surgical excision.
  • Toxoplasma gondii — tissue cysts (bradyzoites) in muscle, brain, eye; usually asymptomatic; reactivation in immunocompromised.
  • Sarcocystis spp. — rare; encyst in skeletal & cardiac muscle; usually asymptomatic; may cause myositis.
  • Trypanosoma cruzi — amastigote forms pseudocysts in cardiac muscle (Chagas disease); not skeletal muscle typically.
  • Gnathostoma spinigerum — larval migration through muscle; visceral & cutaneous larva migrans; eosinophilia.
  • Sparganum (Spirometra) — sparganosis; larval cestode in subcutaneous tissue & muscle; from applying frog/fish flesh to skin or eating undercooked frog/snake/fish.
  • Dracunculus medinensis — Guinea worm; adult worm in subcutaneous tissue (not muscle); emerging through skin blister.

Clinical Pearl

The two most important parasites forming cysts in skeletal muscle are Taenia solium (cysticercosis) and Trichinella spiralis (trichinellosis). Cysticercosis — acquired by ingesting T. solium eggs (faecal-oral); not from eating pork (that causes taeniasis); skeletal muscle cysts are usually asymptomatic but visible on X-ray as elliptical "cigar-shaped" calcifications; neurocysticercosis is the most important manifestation (seizures, headache). Trichinellosis — acquired by eating undercooked pork or wild game (bear, walrus); classic triad of fever, periorbital oedema, & myalgia with eosinophilia; larvae encyst in muscle (diaphragm, extraocular, masseter, tongue); muscle biopsy diagnostic. Always ask about dietary history — undercooked pork/wild game for trichinellosis; exposure to T. solium carrier (food handler) for cysticercosis. Periorbital oedema with eosinophilia & myalgia after pork ingestion = trichinellosis until proven otherwise. "Cigar-shaped" calcifications in muscle on X-ray = cysticercosis. Albendazole is the drug of choice for both; add corticosteroids to prevent inflammatory reaction to dying parasites (especially in neurocysticercosis — dexamethasone before albendazole). India — cysticercosis is endemic (especially UP, Bihar, Punjab, Rajasthan); neurocysticercosis is the most common cause of adult-onset epilepsy. Trichinellosis is rare in India (pork consumption varies by region; religious restrictions in Hindus & Muslims).

Definition

Darling's disease — also called Histoplasmosis — is a systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungus Histoplasma capsulatum. Named after Samuel Darling who described it in 1905 in Panama. Endemic in Ohio & Mississippi River valleys (USA), parts of Central & South America, Africa, India (along Ganges & Brahmaputra riverbeds), SE Asia.

Causative Agent

Histoplasma capsulatum — dimorphic fungus of family Ajellomycetaceae.

  • Mould form (25 °C, environmental):
    • Septate hyphae with microconidia (2–5 µm) — infectious; inhaled.
    • Tuberculate macroconidia (8–15 µm) — characteristic spiny ("sea urchin") appearance; diagnostic on culture.
    • Found in soil enriched with bird/bat guano (chicken coops, starling roosts, bat caves, old buildings).
  • Yeast form (37 °C, host tissue):
    • Small (2–4 µm) oval yeast cells; narrow-based budding.
    • Intracellular — within macrophages ("Histoplasma packed in macrophages looks like cluster of grapes").
    • Found in tissue biopsy, peripheral blood (in disseminated disease), bone marrow.

Two Varieties

  • H. capsulatum var. capsulatum — worldwide (classic histoplasmosis); small yeast (2–4 µm).
  • H. capsulatum var. duboisii — Africa (African histoplasmosis); larger yeast (8–15 µm); cutaneous, subcutaneous, bone lesions predominant.

Transmission

  • Inhalation of microconidia from soil enriched with bird/bat guano — activities like cave exploration (spelunking), chicken farming, cleaning old barns, demolition, excavation.
  • NOT transmitted person-to-person.
  • Incubation — 5–18 days (average 10 days) for acute pulmonary; weeks-months for disseminated.

Clinical Syndromes

Syndrome Features
Acute pulmonary histoplasmosisMost cases asymptomatic. Symptomatic — fever, cough, headache, myalgia, chest pain; patchy pneumonia on CXR; hilar lymphadenopathy. May cause erythema nodosum & arthritis (acute rheumatological). Self-limited in 1–3 weeks.
Severe acute pulmonary (diffuse)Heavy exposure; diffuse reticulonodular infiltrates; hypoxaemia; ARDS; may need antifungals.
Chronic pulmonary histoplasmosisUnderlying lung disease (emphysema); cavitary upper lobe lesions mimicking TB; cough, sputum, weight loss, haemoptysis. Progressive if untreated.
Disseminated histoplasmosisImmunocompromised (HIV with CD4 <100, transplant, steroids); infants; elderly. Fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, pancytopenia, mucocutaneous lesions (oral ulcers), adrenal insufficiency (Addison's), meningitis, endocarditis. Fatal if untreated.
Ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS)Presumed ocular; choroiditis; macular scarring; visual loss.
HistoplasmomaSolitary pulmonary nodule (residual); central calcification ("target lesion"); often incidental finding.
Fibrosing mediastinitisRare; excessive fibrotic response to healed infection; compresses SVC, bronchi, pulmonary vessels.

Pathogenesis

  1. Inhaled microconidia reach alveoli; phagocytosed by macrophages.
  2. Convert to yeast form at 37 °C (dimorphism — virulence factor).
  3. Multiply within macrophages (resist killing by inhibiting phagosome-lysosome fusion; alkalinise phagosome).
  4. Drain to regional lymph nodes → disseminate haematogenously (especially to reticuloendothelial system — liver, spleen, bone marrow) within macrophages.
  5. Cell-mediated immunity (Th1, TNF-α) develops in 2–3 weeks → granuloma formation (caseating); controls infection.
  6. In immunocompromised — uncontrolled replication → disseminated disease.
  7. Calcified granulomas in lung, spleen, liver ("scatterred buckshot" calcifications); heal over years.

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Specimen

  • Sputum, BAL, induced sputum.
  • Blood (EDTA, isolate buffy coat for intracellular yeasts in disseminated disease).
  • Bone marrow aspirate/biopsy.
  • Tissue biopsy — lung, lymph node, liver, skin, oral mucosa.
  • CSF — for meningitis.
  • Urine, serum — for antigen detection.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • Giemsa or Wright stain of peripheral blood smear, bone marrow aspirate, or buffy coat — small (2–4 µm) oval yeast cells inside macrophages ("cluster of grapes"); narrow-based budding.
  • KOH mount — yeast in tissue.
  • Histopathology — H&E shows granuloma (caseating) with yeasts in macrophages; GMS (Grocott methenamine silver) & PAS stain reveal yeasts (2–4 µm, narrow-based budding, surrounded by clear halo — pseudocapsule).

3. Culture

  • Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) with antibiotics (without cycloheximide — inhibits H. capsulatum) — incubate at 25–30 °C for 4–6 weeks (slow grower).
  • BACTEC MGIT, BHI agar.
  • Colony morphology (mould phase at 25 °C) — cottony white to tan/buff colonies; reverse white.
  • Microscopy (lactophenol cotton blue) — septate hyphae with tuberculate macroconidia (8–15 µm, spiny surface — like sea urchin) — pathognomonic; also microconidia (2–5 µm).
  • Conversion to yeast phase — subculture on brain heart infusion (BHI) blood agar at 37 °C; confirms dimorphism.
  • Nucleic acid probe (AccuProbe) — rapid confirmation; species-specific DNA probe hybridisation.
  • Biohazard — mould form highly infectious; BSL-3 lab required for culture.

4. Antigen Detection

  • Histoplasma galactomannan antigen:
    • Detected in urine (most sensitive), serum, BAL, CSF.
    • Sensitivity — 90%+ for disseminated disease; 80% for acute pulmonary; lower for chronic pulmonary.
    • Useful for diagnosis & monitoring treatment response (antigen level falls with effective therapy).
    • Cross-reactivity — Blastomyces (~50%), Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei, Paracoccidioides.

5. Antibody Detection (Serology)

  • Complement fixation (CF):
    • Antibody titres ≥1:32 (yeast antigen) or ≥1:8 (mycelial antigen) suggest active infection.
    • 4-fold rise in paired sera more specific.
    • Sensitivity 80–95%.
  • Immunodiffusion (ID):
    • H & M bands — H band indicates active infection; M band indicates recent or past infection.
    • Specific but less sensitive (70–80%).
  • ELISA — for antibodies; useful for screening.
  • Limitations — antibody response impaired in immunocompromised (HIV); false negative in disseminated disease; positive for years after infection.

6. Molecular Tests

  • PCR — detects H. capsulatum DNA in tissue, blood, BAL; investigational; not widely available.
  • Real-time PCR.

7. Other Tests

  • CBC — pancytopenia in disseminated (bone marrow involvement); anaemia; leucopenia; thrombocytopenia.
  • LFT — elevated (hepatic involvement).
  • Adrenal function — cortisol, ACTH stimulation test (adrenal involvement → Addison's disease).
  • Chest X-ray — patchy pneumonia; hilar lymphadenopathy; cavitary lesions (chronic); miliary pattern (disseminated); calcified nodules (healed).
  • CT chest — more detailed.
  • Skin test (histoplasmin) — for epidemiological surveys (delayed hypersensitivity); not for diagnosis (positive for years after exposure).

Treatment

Syndrome Treatment
Acute pulmonary (mild-moderate)Usually self-limited; rest, NSAIDs. If symptoms >4 weeks: Itraconazole 200 mg TID × 3 days then 200 mg BD × 6–12 weeks.
Severe acute pulmonaryLiposomal Amphotericin B 3 mg/kg/day × 2 weeks → Itraconazole × 12 weeks.
Chronic pulmonaryItraconazole 200 mg BD × 12–24 months.
Disseminated (moderate-severe)Liposomal Amphotericin B 3 mg/kg/day × 2 weeks → Itraconazole 200 mg BD × ≥12 months.
Disseminated (mild)Itraconazole 200 mg BD × 12 months.
MeningitisLiposomal Amphotericin B 5 mg/kg/day × 4–6 weeks → Itraconazole × 12 months (or longer).
HIV (maintenance)Itraconazole lifelong OR secondary prophylaxis until immune reconstitution on ART (CD4 >150 for 6 months).

Prevention

  • Avoid areas with high bird/bat guano — caves, chicken coops, old buildings.
  • Wear N95 mask, protective clothing when cleaning chicken coops, exploring caves, demolishing old buildings.
  • Wet soil before excavation to reduce dust.
  • Prophylaxis — Itraconazole for immunocompromised (HIV with CD4 <150) in endemic areas (controversial).
  • No vaccine available.

Clinical Pearl

Think histoplasmosis in any patient with prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, & mucocutaneous lesions — especially if immunocompromised (HIV with CD4 <100) or from endemic area (Ohio-Mississippi valley, India's Ganges belt). The buffy coat of peripheral blood or bone marrow aspirate stained with Giemsa showing small (2–4 µm) intracellular yeasts in macrophages is the most rapid diagnostic test for disseminated disease. Histoplasma antigen in urine is the most sensitive non-culture test (90%+); falls with treatment response — useful for monitoring. Adrenal involvement is common — bilateral adrenal enlargement; may cause Addison's disease (check cortisol, ACTH stimulation). Distinguish from TB — both cause granulomatous disease with similar features; culture or antigen detection is essential. India — endemic along Ganges (UP, Bihar, Bengal) & Brahmaputra (Assam) riverbeds; bat caves in Andamans; underdiagnosed. The tuberculate macroconidia on culture (25 °C) are pathognomonic — spiny "sea urchin" appearance. Mould form is highly infectious to laboratory workers — BSL-3 required for culture; opening a Petri dish of mould-form H. capsulatum can cause laboratory-acquired infection. Itraconazole is the oral drug of choice; liposomal amphotericin B for severe disease. Monitor itraconazole levels — ensure therapeutic; check drug interactions (CYP3A4 — many). HIV patients need lifelong secondary prophylaxis until CD4 >150 for 6 months on ART.

Introduction

Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus, GAS) — Gram-positive cocci in chains, β-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive — is a pyogenic (pus-forming) pathogen causing a wide spectrum of suppurative (purulent) infections of skin, soft tissue, respiratory tract, & systemic sites.

1. Pharyngitis ("Strep Throat") — Most Common

  • Acute inflammation of pharynx & tonsils.
  • Clinical — sudden onset sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough/coryza (Centor criteria).
  • Complications — peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), retropharyngeal abscess, otitis media, sinusitis, meningitis.
  • Non-suppurative sequelae — acute rheumatic fever (ARF), post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).
  • Diagnosis — throat swab culture (blood agar — β-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive); rapid antigen detection test (RADT); ASO titre.
  • Treatment — oral penicillin V or amoxicillin × 10 days; azithromycin if allergic.

2. Impetigo (Pyoderma)

  • Superficial skin infection; two forms:
    • Non-bullous impetigo — most common; honey-coloured crusts on erythematous base; face, extremities; common in children.
    • Bullous impetigo — flaccid bullae that rupture, leaving thin flat varnish-like crust; caused by S. aureus exfoliative toxin A/B (less commonly GAS).
    • Ecthyma — deeper ulcerative form; punched-out ulcers with necrotic scab; legs.
  • Complications — cellulitis, lymphangitis; PSGN (especially M type 49).
  • Treatment — topical mupirocin; oral antibiotics (cephalexin, dicloxacillin) for extensive.

3. Cellulitis & Erysipelas

  • Cellulitis — deep dermal & subcutaneous infection; spreading erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness, indistinct margins; lower limbs common; portal of entry (fissure, ulcer, trauma, tinea pedis).
  • Erysipelas — more superficial; raised, sharply demarcated borders; "orange-peel" appearance; face (classic), legs.
  • Complications — abscess, necrotising fasciitis, bacteraemia, sepsis.
  • Treatment — oral dicloxacillin/cephalexin; IV for severe, diabetic, immunocompromised.

4. Necrotising Fasciitis ("Flesh-Eating Disease")

  • Rapidly progressive necrosis of subcutaneous tissue & fascia; spreads along fascial planes.
  • Two types:
    • Type II (monomicrobial) — S. pyogenes (GAS) — classic "flesh-eating" form; often with STSS; trauma, surgery, IV drug use; rapid progression (hours).
    • Type I (polymicrobial) — mixed aerobes & anaerobes; perineum (Fournier gangrene), diabetic foot, post-surgical.
  • Clinical — severe pain out of proportion to findings; erythema, swelling, crepitus (gas), skin discolouration (purple/grey), bullae, necrosis; systemic toxicity; septic shock.
  • Complications — Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome (STSS); multi-organ failure; limb loss; death (mortality 20–40%).
  • Treatment — emergency surgical debridement (life-saving); IV penicillin + clindamycin (suppresses toxin); IVIG; supportive ICU.

  • Puerperal sepsis (post-partum endometritis — historical "childbed fever").
  • Surgical wound infection.
  • Septic arthritis, osteomyelitis (less common than S. aureus).
  • Pneumonia (post-viral, e.g., after influenza/measles).
  • Meningitis, brain abscess (rare).
  • Peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, Ludwig's angina.
  • Otitis media, sinusitis.
  • Bacteraemia, sepsis, STSS.

Clinical Pearl

S. pyogenes (GAS) is one of the few bacteria capable of causing the full spectrum from trivial (impetigo, pharyngitis) to life-threatening (necrotising fasciitis, STSS). The key virulence factor is the M protein — anti-phagocytic; antibodies against M protein are protective but specific to serotype (so recurrent infections with different serotypes possible). Always consider GAS in any rapidly progressive soft tissue infection — pain out of proportion to findings, systemic toxicity, rapid spread → necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise; emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin + clindamycin. Penicillin remains the drug of choice — no resistance reported in GAS; macrolide resistance ~5–20%. Lepromatous leprosy (LL) — the multibacillary, anergic pole of the leprosy spectrum — occurs in hosts with weak cell-mediated (Th1) immunity & strong humoral (Th2) response. Bacilli multiply unchecked; high bacterial load; systemic involvement.

1. Skin Lesions — Multiple, Symmetric, Diffuse

  • Multiple, symmetrical, bilateral distribution — face, trunk, extremities.
  • Macules, papules, plaques, nodules — erythematous or copper-coloured; poorly defined (unlike tuberculoid — sharply defined).
  • Diffuse infiltration of skin — thickened, waxy, doughy texture.
  • Leonine facies — coarse, furrowed facial skin with nodular infiltration (forehead, eyebrows, cheeks, nose, ears) — "lion-like" appearance; classic.

  • Saddle-nose deformity — destruction of nasal cartilage.
  • Pendulous ear lobes.
  • Hypopigmentation (mild — lesions not sharply demarcated).
  • Sensation relatively preserved early (unlike TT — anaesthesia is late in LL).

2. Nerve Involvement — Symmetric, Widespread, Glove-Stocking Pattern

  • Symmetric peripheral neuropathy — glove & stocking anaesthesia; distal > proximal.
  • Multiple nerves thickened — great auricular, ulnar, radial cutaneous, common peroneal, posterior tibial; palpable, tender.
  • Claw hand (ulnar), foot drop (peroneal), claw toes (posterior tibial), lagophthalmos & corneal anaesthesia (facial nerve) — late.
  • Trophic ulcers — painless plantar ulcers; autoamputation of digits.
  • Nerve damage is slower than in TT but more widespread.

3. Mucosal Involvement — Nasal, Oral, Laryngeal

  • Nasal mucosa — earliest & most common; nasal stuffiness, epistaxis, discharge (highly bacillated — "lepromatous nodules"); perforation of nasal septum → saddle nose; collapse of nasal bridge.
  • Oral mucosa — nodular infiltration of palate, uvula, tongue; ulceration; tooth loss.
  • Larynx — hoarseness, stridor; nodular infiltration of epiglottis, vocal cords.

  • Very high bacterial load — skin smears strongly positive (BI 4–6+); globi (clusters of bacilli in foamy macrophages / Virchow cells) on microscopy — pathognomonic.
  • Lymphadenopathy — generalised; bacilli in nodes.
  • Hepatosplenomegaly — reticuloendothelial involvement.
  • Testicular involvement — orchitis, infertility, gynaecomastia (↓testosterone, ↑oestrogen from testicular damage).
  • Eye — uveitis, keratitis, blindness.
  • Bone — periostitis, osteitis, absorption of digits.
  • Kidney — amyloidosis (secondary AA); glomerulonephritis.
  • Reactions — Type 2 (ENL — erythema nodosum leprosum) common in LL.

  • Lepromin (Mitsuda) test — negative (absent CMI against M. leprae).
  • Serology (PGL-1 IgM) — strongly positive.
  • Histology — diffuse infiltrate of foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) loaded with bacilli (globi); Grenz zone (subepidermal clear zone separating infiltrate from atrophic epidermis); few lymphocytes; no granuloma (unlike TT).
  • Eye involvement — uveitis, episcleritis, keratitis, lagophthalmos leading to exposure keratitis & blindness.
  • Immunology — anergy to M. leprae (specific); normal immunity to other antigens; high antibody levels (IgM anti-PGL-1) but no protection (humoral response ineffective against intracellular pathogen).

  • MB-MDT (Multibacillary regimen) — Rifampicin 600 mg + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100 mg + Clofazimine 50 mg daily (self-administered) × 12 months.

  • Long-term follow-up — relapse, deformity, reactions.

Clinical Pearl

The leonine facies (coarse furrowed face with nodular infiltration) is the classic physical sign of lepromatous leprosy — combined with madarosis (eyebrow loss) & saddle nose deformity, the diagnosis is clinical. Symmetrical multiple skin lesions with relatively preserved sensation early (anaesthesia develops late in LL) distinguishes LL from tuberculoid leprosy (TT — single/few sharply defined anaesthetic lesions). Skin smear strongly positive (BI 4–6+) with globi (clusters of bacilli in Virchow cells) — pathognomonic. Lepromin test is negative (absent CMI); serology (PGL-1 IgM) strongly positive. Histology shows foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) with Grenz zone — no granuloma. Nasal mucosa is the primary site & source of transmission — bacilli shed in nasal discharge; highly infectious. Type 2 reaction (ENL) — crops of painful erythematous nodules on face & extensor surfaces; fever, malaise, neuritis, iritis, orchitis, dactylitis; treat with thalidomide (strictly avoid in pregnancy — severe phocomelia) or prednisolone. Always check for systemic involvement — eye (uveitis, blindness), testis (infertility, gynaecomastia), kidney (amyloidosis). MB-MDT for 12 months — rifampicin kills 99.9% of bacilli with single dose; clofazimine anti-inflammatory; dapsone antibacterial. Introduction

Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) — Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci, α-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble — causes pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, sinusitis, bacteraemia. Virulence factors enable colonisation, evasion of host defences, & tissue invasion.

Two Important Virulence Factors

1. Polysaccharide Capsule — Most Important

  • Structure — thick polysaccharide capsule surrounding cell wall; capsular serotype determines antigenicity (>90 serotypes identified; ~13 covered by PCV13 vaccine, 23 by PPSV23).
  • Mechanism:
    • Anti-phagocytic — prevents opsonisation by complement & antibodies; resists phagocytosis by neutrophils & macrophages.
    • Hinders complement activation — capsule impairs C3b deposition on bacterial surface; alternative pathway less effective.
    • Resists mucosal clearance — facilitates colonisation of nasopharynx & invasion.
    • Strains without capsule (rough colonies) are non-pathogenic — avirulent.
  • Protection — type-specific IgG antibodies against capsule → opsonisation → phagocytosis. Basis of pneumococcal vaccines (PCV13 — conjugate; PPSV23 — polysaccharide).
  • Serotype distribution — 6A, 6B, 9V, 14, 19A, 19F, 23F most common in children; 3, 4, 6B, 9V, 14, 19F, 23F in adults.
  • Serotype replacement — after PCV7 introduction, non-vaccine serotypes (especially 19A, 6A) emerged; PCV13 expanded coverage.

2. Pneumolysin — Cytolytic Toxin

  • Structure — 53 kDa cholesterol-dependent cytolysin (CDC); produced by virtually all pneumococcal strains; intracellular (released on autolysis).
  • Mechanism:
    • Pore formation — binds cholesterol in host cell membranes → oligomerises → forms transmembrane pores (β-barrel) → osmotic lysis & cell death.
    • Haemolysis — lyses RBCs (α-haemolysis on blood agar — partial; pneumolysin contributes; also O₂-labile pneumolysin — enhanced under anaerobic conditions).
    • Cytotoxic to ciliated epithelium — damages respiratory epithelium; impairs mucociliary clearance.
    • Complement activation — classical pathway (binds Fc portion of IgG); depletes complement; reduces opsonisation.
    • Pro-inflammatory — activates NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β release; neutrophil recruitment.
    • Neurotoxic — damages brain microvascular endothelial cells; contributes to meningitis pathogenesis & hearing loss.
    • Cardiotoxic — damages myocardium; contributes to cardiac complications of pneumococcal pneumonia.
  • Role in disease — worsens pneumonia severity; meningitis; otitis media; invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD).

Other Virulence Factors

  • Surface proteins:
    • Pneumococcal surface protein A (PspA) — anti-complement; anti-phagocytic; vaccine candidate.
    • Pneumococcal surface protein C (PspC / CbpA) — binds polymeric Ig receptor & factor H; colonisation & immune evasion.
    • Pneumococcal surface antigen A (PsaA) — manganese transporter; adhesion; vaccine candidate.
    • Choline-binding proteins — adhere to epithelial cells (CbpA).
  • Cell wall components:
    • Teichoic acid — activates complement; pro-inflammatory (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).
    • Peptidoglycan — activates alternative complement; cytokine release.
    • C-polysaccharide — activates CRP (C-reactive protein) in host.
  • Enzymes:
    • IgA1 protease — cleaves host secretory IgA1; evades mucosal immunity; facilitates colonisation.
    • Neuraminidase (NanA, NanB, NanC) — cleaves sialic acid from host glycoproteins; exposes receptors for adhesion; contributes to otitis media & meningitis.
    • Hyaluronidase — tissue invasion.
    • Autolysin (LytA) — causes bacterial lysis at stationary phase → releases pneumolysin & cell wall components; contributes to inflammation & virulence.
  • Pili (type IV) — adhesion to epithelial cells; colonisation; some strains only.

Clinical Pearl

The polysaccharide capsule is the single most important virulence factor of S. pneumoniae — strains without capsule are non-pathogenic; antibodies against capsule (opsonising IgG) are protective; basis of pneumococcal vaccines. >90 capsular serotypes identified — vaccine covers subset (PCV13: 13 serotypes causing >80% of invasive disease in children; PPSV23: 23 serotypes for adults). Serotype replacement — non-vaccine serotypes emerge after vaccination (especially 19A after PCV7; replaced by PCV13); ongoing surveillance essential. Pneumolysin — pore-forming toxin; cytotoxic to respiratory epithelium, RBC, neurons, myocardium; worsens severity; vaccine candidate. IgA1 protease — cleaves secretory IgA1; evades mucosal immunity — explains high colonisation rate in children. Always suspect S. pneumoniae in: acute community-acquired pneumonia (rusty sputum), acute bacterial meningitis (Gram-positive diplococci in CSF), otitis media in children, sinusitis, bacteraemia in asplenic patients. Optochin sensitivity — pneumococcus sensitive (≥14 mm zone); viridans streptococci resistant. India — PCV13 introduced in UIP (2017); reduces pneumococcal pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, & antimicrobial resistance.
