Introduction

Staphylococcus aureus — Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive — produces a remarkable array of virulence factors. Here are two of the most important.

Two Virulence Factors of Staphylococcus

1. Coagulase — Free & Bound

  • Free coagulase (secreted enzyme):
    • Activates prothrombin → thrombin → converts fibrinogen → fibrin → clot formation.
    • Walls off infection → abscess formation; protects bacteria from phagocytes & antibiotics.
    • Tube coagulase test detects this; definitive for S. aureus identification.
  • Bound coagulase (clumping factor):
    • Surface protein (ClfA, ClfB) that binds fibrinogen directly → fibrin coat on bacterial surface.
    • Resists phagocytosis.
    • Slide coagulase test detects this.
  • Role in disease — abscess formation (boils, carbuncles, abscesses); endocarditis (vegetation); foreign body infection (biofilm on catheter); distinguishes S. aureus from CoNS.

2. Protein A — Surface Protein

  • Structure — 42 kDa cell wall surface protein anchored to peptidoglycan; expressed by all S. aureus strains.
  • Mechanism:
    • Binds Fc portion of IgG in wrong orientation — the Fab (antigen-binding) ends face outward, Fc faces inward.
    • Prevents opsonisation — phagocytes cannot recognise Fc.
    • Resists phagocytosis by neutrophils & macrophages.
    • Also a B-cell superantigen — binds VH3 region of B-cell receptor → polyclonal B-cell activation → immune evasion.
  • Role in disease — major immune evasion mechanism; enables colonisation & invasive infection; basis for clinical identification (staphylococcal slide agglutination tests — bound protein A & clumping factor detected simultaneously).
  • Clinical use — protein A columns used therapeutically to remove IgG-mediated antibodies (immunoadsorption) in autoimmune disease (ITP, myasthenia gravis, SLE).

  • Hemolysins — α-toxin (pore-forming; dermonecrotic), β-haemolysin (sphingomyelinase), γ-haemolysin, δ-toxin.
  • Leucocidins — Panton-Valentine leucocidin (PVL — destroys neutrophils; CA-MRSA; necrotising pneumonia); LukAB, LukED.
  • Superantigens — TSST-1 (toxic shock syndrome), enterotoxins A–U (food poisoning), exfoliative toxins A & B (scalded skin syndrome).
  • Capsule — anti-phagocytic (type 5 & 8).
  • Teichoic acid — adherence to mucosa & prosthetic devices.
  • Catalase — neutralises H₂O₂ (survives neutrophil oxidative burst).
  • Enzymes — hyaluronidase ("spreading factor"), fibrinolysin, DNase, lipase, protease.
  • Biofilm — polysaccharide intercellular adhesin (PIA); device infections.
  • Antibiotic resistance — β-lactamase (penicillin resistance); PBP2a/mecA (MRSA).

The coagulase test is the single most important lab test to differentiate S. aureus (positive) from coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS — S. epidermidis, S. saprophyticus). Protein A is unique to S. aureus — binds Fc of IgG in wrong orientation, preventing opsonisation; enables the bacteria to evade phagocytosis & complement; basis for slide agglutination tests. Acute pyogenic (septic) arthritis in sexually active young adults has a distinctive microbiology — sexually transmitted pathogens predominate. The two most important causative agents are Neisseria gonorrhoeae (most common) & Chlamydia trachomatis.

    • Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI) — two clinical forms:

Introduction

Clostridium tetani — Gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming, drumstick-shaped bacillus — produces two potent exotoxins. The most important is tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin) — responsible for clinical tetanus.

Two Toxins of C. tetani

1. Tetanospasmin (Tetanus Toxin, TeNT) — Most Important

  • Structure:
    • 150 kDa A-B toxin (similar to botulinum, diphtheria toxins).
    • Single polypeptide; cleaved by protease into:
      • Heavy chain (100 kDa, B subunit) — binding & translocation; binds neurons; mediates entry.
      • Light chain (50 kDa, A subunit) — active moiety; Zn²⁺-dependent endopeptidase (metalloprotease).
    • Linked by disulfide bond.
  • Mechanism of action:
    1. Toxin released at site of infection; enters peripheral motor neurons (via SV2A/SV2B receptor + polysialogangliosides on neuron surface).
    2. Retrograde axonal transport to spinal cord (anterior horn) & brainstem.
    3. Heavy chain mediates translocation across synaptic membrane into synaptosome.
    4. Light chain cleaves SNARE protein synaptobrevin (VAMP-2) — vesicle-associated membrane protein.
    5. Cleaved synaptobrevin cannot mediate vesicle fusion → prevents release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA & glycine) from interneurons (Renshaw cells) onto motor neurons.
    6. Loss of inhibition → uncontrolled motor neuron firing → severe sustained muscle spasms.
  • Clinical effects:
    • Trismus (lockjaw) — masseter spasm; earliest sign.
    • Risus sardonicus — sardonic smile from facial muscle spasm.
    • Opisthotonus — arching of back; severe hyperextension.
    • Generalised tetanus — sustained muscle spasms; respiratory compromise; autonomic dysfunction (sympathetic overactivity — labile BP, arrhythmias); intact sensorium.
    • Cephalic tetanus — cranial nerve palsies (especially VII) after head/face wound or otitis media.
    • Neonatal tetanus — from unsterile umbilical cord care.
    • Mortality 10–40% even with treatment; near 100% untreated.
  • Treatment:
    • HTIG (Human Tetanus Immune Globulin) 3000–6000 IU IM/IV — neutralises unbound toxin only (does NOT reverse bound toxin).
    • IV Metronidazole × 7–10 days — kills organism.
    • Surgical debridement of wound.
    • Supportive — diazepam (muscle relaxant), mechanical ventilation, magnesium sulphate (autonomic dysfunction).
    • Active immunisation with TT (tetanus toxoid) at recovery — clinical tetanus does NOT confer immunity (toxin amount too small).
  • Prevention:
    • Tetanus toxoid (TT) vaccine — formaldehyde-treated toxin; loses toxicity but retains antigenicity; adsorbed on aluminium hydroxide.
    • Given as DTP/DTaP/Tdap/Td in childhood & adulthood.
    • India — 3 primary doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks; boosters at 16–18 months & 5 years; Td at 10 & 16 years; adults every 10 years.
    • Pregnancy — Td in each pregnancy.

  • Structure:
    • 49 kDa cholesterol-dependent cytolysin (CDC).
    • Oxygen-labile (inactivated by O₂); heat-labile.
    • Member of cholesterol-binding toxin family (similar to streptolysin O, pneumolysin, listeriolysin O, perfringolysin O).
  • Mechanism:
    1. Binds cholesterol in host cell membranes.
    2. Oligomerises into ring-shaped pre-pore (40–50 monomers).
    3. Undergoes conformational change → inserts into membrane → forms transmembrane β-barrel pore (large; 30 nm diameter).
    4. Osmotic lysis & cell death.
  • Effects:
    • Haemolysis — lyses RBCs; contributes to local tissue destruction.
    • Cytotoxic — damages leukocytes, macrophages, platelets, myocardium (in vitro).
    • Degranulation of mast cells & platelets.
    • Complement activation — classical pathway.
  • Role in disease — uncertain; less important than tetanospasmin; may contribute to local necrosis & create anaerobic environment favourable for C. tetani growth; may aid in iron acquisition (from lysed RBCs).
  • Antigenically related to streptolysin O, pneumolysin — anti-tetanolysin antibodies cross-react.

Tetanospasmin (TeNT) is one of the most potent toxins known — minimum lethal dose in humans ~2.5 ng/kg; acts by cleaving synaptobrevin (VAMP-2) → blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA & glycine) → uncontrolled motor neuron firing → tetanus. Introduction

Acute gastroenteritis is a leading cause of childhood mortality globally, especially in developing countries. Viruses are the most common cause in children <5 years. The two most important are Rotavirus (most common cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea) & Norovirus (most common cause of outbreaks / sporadic gastroenteritis).

Two Common Viruses Causing Acute Gastroenteritis in Young Children

1. Rotavirus — Most Common Cause of Severe Dehydrating Diarrhoea

  • Family: Reoviridae; genus Rotavirus.
  • Structure:
    • Non-enveloped; icosahedral; double capsid (triple-layered).
    • Wheel-like appearance ("rota" = wheel) under electron microscopy.
    • Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); 11 segments.
    • Outer capsid proteins — VP4 (P-type protease-sensitive) & VP7 (G-type glycoprotein) — define serotype; basis of vaccine strains.
    • Inner capsid — VP6 (most abundant; antigenic; defines group A–G; Group A most common in humans).
  • Transmission — faecal-oral; contaminated food/water; fomites; respiratory droplets (possible).
  • Incubation — 1–3 days.
  • Pathogenesis:
    1. Virus ingested → infects mature enterocytes of small intestinal villi (especially proximal small intestine).
    2. VP4 binds enterocyte receptors (integrins, gangliosides, HbA).
    3. VP4 cleaved by intestinal trypsin → enhances infectivity.
    4. Virus enters cell; replicates in cytoplasm.
    5. NSP4 (non-structural protein 4) — enterotoxin; triggers calcium influx → chloride secretion → watery diarrhoea; also induces apoptosis of enterocytes.
    6. Destruction of mature absorptive enterocytes → villous atrophy; malabsorption; decreased disaccharidases (especially lactase) → osmotic diarrhoea.
    7. Resolves in 5–7 days; lifelong immunity develops (but multiple serotypes possible reinfection).
  • Clinical features:
    • Sudden onset fever, vomiting (prominent; 1–2 days), profuse watery diarrhoea (5–10 days).
    • Dehydration — mild to severe; leading cause of hospitalisation in infants <2 yr.
    • Seizures (febrile) in some children.
    • Death from dehydration & electrolyte imbalance if untreated.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Stool antigen ELISA (VP6) — most common; rapid (15 min); high sensitivity/specificity.
    • Latex agglutination, immunochromatographic rapid tests.
    • PAGE (polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis) of stool RNA — characteristic 11-segment pattern ("electropherotype").
    • RT-PCR — gold standard; detects & genotypes.
    • Electron microscopy — wheel-like particles.
    • Stool microscopy — no RBCs or WBCs (non-invasive).
  • Treatment:
    • ORS (oral rehydration solution) — WHO formula; low-osmolarity (Na 75, glucose 75 mmol/L) — mainstay.
    • IV fluids (Ringer's lactate) for severe dehydration.
    • Zinc supplementation — 20 mg/day × 10–14 days; reduces duration & severity; WHO recommended.
    • Probiotics (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG).
    • No antivirals; avoid antimotility agents.
  • Prevention:
    • Rotavirus vaccine:
      • Rotarix (RV1) — monovalent; G1P[8]; 2 doses at 6 & 10 weeks (or 6 & 14 weeks).
      • RotaTeq (RV5) — pentavalent; G1, G2, G3, G4, P[8]; 3 doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks.
      • ROTAVAC (116E) — Indian indigenous (Bharat Biotech); neonatal strain; 3 doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks.
      • ROTASIIL — Indian (Serum Institute); thermostable; lyophilised; 3 doses.
      • India — included in UIP (2016); reduced rotavirus diarrhoea mortality by ~50%.
      • Contraindication — severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID); history of intussusception.
      • Small increased risk of intussusception (~1 in 50,000–100,000) — benefit outweighs risk.
    • Hand hygiene, safe water, sanitation, exclusive breastfeeding (6 months).

  • Family: Caliciviridae; genus Norovirus.
  • Structure:
    • Non-enveloped; icosahedral; small (27–40 nm).

    • Positive-sense single-stranded RNA (+ssRNA).
    • Single major capsid protein (VP1) + minor VP2.
    • Genogroups GI, GII (most common in humans); GIV.

    • Faecal-oral — contaminated food (shellfish, salads, fruits, ready-to-eat food handled by infected food handler).
    • Person-to-person — direct contact; aerosolised vomitus.
    • Fomites — surfaces (door handles, keyboards); survives 7 days on surfaces.
    • Waterborne — recreational water, drinking water.
  • Incubation — 12–48 h.
  • Infective dose — very low (~18 viral particles); highly contagious.
  • Pathogenesis:
    1. Virus infects mature enterocytes of proximal small intestine (jejunum).
    2. Receptors — histo-blood group antigens (HBGA); secretor status determines susceptibility.
    3. Villus blunting; crypt hyperplasia; transient malabsorption.
    4. Inflammatory response — minimal (no RBCs/WBCs in stool).
    5. Decreased brush border enzymes (lactase, sucrase, maltase) → osmotic diarrhoea.
    6. Delayed gastric emptying → vomiting.

  • Clinical features:
    • Acute onset nausea, vomiting (prominent), abdominal cramps, watery diarrhoea.

    • RT-PCR (real-time) — gold standard; detects & genotypes.
    • ELISA for norovirus antigen — rapid.
    • Electron microscopy — small round structured viruses (SRSV).

Virus Features

AstrovirusMild; infants <2 yr; winter; 2–4 days
Sapovirus (Caliciviridae)Milder than norovirus; outbreaks & sporadic

Rotavirus is the most common cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in children <5 yr — responsible for ~40% of hospitalisations for childhood gastroenteritis globally; mortality ~200,000/year (mostly developing countries). Introduction

Influenza virus — family Orthomyxoviridae — undergoes two types of antigenic variation that allow it to evade host immunity & cause recurrent epidemics & pandemics: antigenic drift & antigenic shift.

Two Antigenic Variants of Influenza Virus

1. Antigenic Drift — Minor Variation (Point Mutations)

  • Mechanism:
    • Point mutations in genes encoding surface antigens haemagglutinin (HA) & neuraminidase (NA).
    • Due to error-prone RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (no proofreading) — mutation rate ~1 in 10,000 nucleotides per replication.
    • Single amino acid changes alter antigenic sites.
    • Selection pressure from host antibodies selects for escape mutants.
  • Frequency — continuous; ongoing every flu season.
  • Magnitude — minor (<1% amino acid change per year).
  • Clinical consequence:
    • Causes annual seasonal epidemics.
    • Reduced vaccine effectiveness — reason annual flu vaccine update needed.
    • Reinfection possible throughout life — partial immunity from prior exposure is incomplete.
  • Strains affected — all types (A, B, C); influenza B undergoes only drift (no shift).
  • Example — H3N2 A/Hong Kong/4801/2014 → A/Singapore/INFIMH-16-0019/2016 (drifted variant of same H3N2).

2. Antigenic Shift — Major Variation (Gene Reassortment)

  • Mechanism:
    • Gene reassortment in cells co-infected with two different influenza A strains (human + animal — avian, swine).
    • Influenza A genome has 8 segmented RNA strands — when two strains infect same cell, segments can re assort into new combinations.
    • Result — novel HA &/or NA subtype to which humans have no prior immunity.
  • Frequency — rare; only occasionally (every 10–40 years).
  • Magnitude — major (new HA or NA subtype — e.g., H1 → H2, H2 → H3).
  • Clinical consequence:
    • Causes pandemics — global spread due to lack of population immunity.
    • Higher mortality than seasonal flu.
    • Vaccine needs complete reformulation based on new strain.
  • Strains affected — influenza A only (B & C infect humans only — no animal reservoir for reassortment).
  • Animal reservoirs:
    • Birds (especially aquatic birds — ducks, geese, shorebirds) — natural reservoir of all 16 HA & 9 NA subtypes.
    • Pigs — "mixing vessel" — susceptible to both avian & human strains → reassortment.
  • Historical pandemics:
    • 1918 — Spanish flu (H1N1) — 50–100 million deaths; avian origin; young adults most affected.
    • 1957 — Asian flu (H2N2) — replaced H1N1; 1–2 million deaths.
    • 1968 — Hong Kong flu (H3N2) — replaced H2N2; 1 million deaths.
    • 1977 — Russian flu (H1N1) — re-emergence of H1N1 (laboratory strain?); co-circulated with H3N2 since.
    • 2009 — Swine flu (H1N1pdm09) — quadruple reassortant (swine + avian + human genes); ~280,000 deaths globally.

Comparison: Drift vs Shift

MechanismPoint mutations in HA/NA genesGene reassortment between strains
FrequencyContinuous; every seasonRare; every 10–40 years
MagnitudeMinor — small antigenic changesMajor — new HA/NA subtype
Virus types affectedA, B, CA only (B & C have no animal reservoir)
Clinical effectSeasonal epidemics; annual vaccine updatePandemics; novel vaccine
Population immunityPartial — cross-protection someNone — pandemic potential

  • Haemagglutinin (HA):
    • 16 subtypes in birds (H1–H16); H1, H2, H3 common in humans.
    • Binds sialic acid receptors on host cells (α2,6 in human upper respiratory tract; α2,3 in birds & human lower respiratory tract).
    • Mediates viral entry & fusion.
    • Major target of neutralising antibodies.
  • Neuraminidase (NA):
    • 9 subtypes (N1–N9); N1 & N2 common in humans.
    • Cleaves sialic acid → releases new virions from infected cells → spreads infection.
    • Target of antiviral drugs — oseltamivir, zanamivir (NA inhibitors).

  • Trivalent — H1N1, H3N2, B/Victoria (or B/Yamagata).
  • Quadrivalent — adds second B lineage.
  • Updated annually by WHO based on global surveillance (Northern & Southern hemisphere strains).
  • Types — inactivated (IM); live attenuated (intranasal — LAIV); high-dose for elderly; adjuvanted; cell-based.

Clinical Pearl

Antigenic drift causes annual seasonal epidemics — minor mutations in HA & NA selected by antibody pressure; reason flu vaccine must be updated every year. Antigenic shift causes pandemics — gene reassortment between human & animal strains (especially in pigs — "mixing vessel") creates novel HA/NA combination to which humans have no immunity; reason pandemic preparedness is critical. Only influenza A undergoes shift — B & C have no animal reservoir. The 1918 Spanish flu (H1N1) killed 50–100 million — more than WWI; avian origin without reassortment (entire avian virus adapted to humans). The 2009 swine flu (H1N1pdm09) was a quadruple reassortant — North American swine, North American avian, human, Eurasian swine genes; replaced seasonal H1N1; now circulates as seasonal H1N1. Avian influenza H5N1 & H7N9 — zoonotic (bird-to-human); high mortality (60% for H5N1) but no sustained human-to-human transmission yet; pandemic potential if they acquire human-transmissible mutations. Annual flu vaccine — best protection; updated based on WHO global surveillance; quadrivalent preferred (covers both B lineages); effectiveness varies (30–60%) due to drift & strain mismatch. Antivirals — oseltamivir, zanamivir (NA inhibitors) — reduce severity & duration if started within 48 h; adamantanes (amantadine, rimantadine) — no longer recommended (resistance in H1N1 & H3N2). India — annual seasonal flu vaccine recommended for high-risk groups (elderly, chronic illness, pregnancy, healthcare workers); H1N1pdm09 (swine flu) outbreaks common.

Introduction

Zoonoses are diseases transmitted from animals to humans. Bacterial zoonoses are common in India due to close human-animal contact (agriculture, livestock, slaughterhouse, veterinary). Here are two important ones.

Two Zoonotic Bacterial Diseases

1. Brucellosis (Brucella spp.)

  • Causative organism:
    • Brucella abortus — cattle; most common worldwide.
    • Brucella melitensis — sheep & goats; most virulent; most common in India, Mediterranean, Middle East.
    • Brucella suis — pigs.
    • Brucella canis — dogs.
  • Gram-negative, intracellular coccobacillus; aerobic; non-motile; non-spore-forming.
  • Transmission:
    • Ingestion of unpasteurised dairy — most common (raw milk, cheese, butter from infected animals).
    • Direct contact with infected animal tissues — farmers, veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers, hunters; through skin abrasions; placenta/aborted foetus highly infectious.
    • Inhalation of aerosols — laboratory workers; slaughterhouse.
    • NOT person-to-person (except rare transfusion, organ transplant, sexual).
  • Incubation — 1–3 weeks (range 5 days to months).
  • Clinical features:
    • Insidious onset — fever (undulant — rises in evening, falls in morning), chills, malaise, fatigue, headache, myalgia, anorexia, weight loss; sweats (characteristic — malodorous, "mouldy hay" smell).
    • osteoarticular — arthritis (sacroiliitis, spondylitis), osteomyelitis; most common focal complication.
    • Genitourinary — epididymo-orchitis (unilateral); abortion in pregnant women & animals.
    • Hepatosplenomegaly; lymphadenopathy.
    • Endocarditis (rare; caused by B. melitensis; life-threatening).
    • Neurobrucellosis — meningitis, encephalitis, depression.
    • Chronic brucellosis — persists >1 year; fatigue, low-grade fever.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Blood culture — gold standard; Castaneda method (biphasic — solid + liquid); BACTEC; positive in 50–70%; incubate 4–6 weeks (slow growing); BSL-3 required (laboratory-acquired infection risk).
    • Serology:
      • Rose Bengal test — rapid screening; agglutination.
      • Standard Agglutination Test (SAT) — quantitative; titre ≥1:160 significant; gold standard serology; cross-reacts with Vibrio cholerae, Yersinia enterocolitica O9, Francisella tularensis, E. coli O157.
      • 2-Mercaptoethanol (2-ME) test — detects IgG (eliminates IgM); indicates active infection.
      • ELISA — IgM, IgG; sensitive.
      • Coombs test — for blocking antibodies in chronic brucellosis.
    • PCR — rapid; species-specific; IS711, bcsp31; blood, tissue.
    • Bone marrow culture — higher yield than blood.
    • CBG — leucopenia, relative lymphocytosis, thrombocytopenia.
    • LFT — mild elevation.
  • Treatment:
    • Adults — Doxycycline 100 mg BD + Rifampicin 600 mg OD × 6 weeks; OR Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 6 weeks + Streptomycin 1 g IM daily × 2–3 weeks (preferred for spondylitis/endocarditis).
    • Children <8 yr — Cotrimoxazole + Rifampicin × 6 weeks.
    • Pregnancy — Rifampicin 900 mg OD × 6 weeks; or cotrimoxazole (avoid 3rd trimester — kernicterus).
    • Endocarditis, neurobrucellosis — triple therapy (doxycycline + rifampicin + cotrimoxazole or aminoglycoside) × 3–6 months.
    • Relapse rate 5–15%.
  • Prevention:
    • Pasteurisation of milk & milk products.
    • Vaccinate cattle (B. abortus RB51) & sheep/goats (B. melitensis Rev-1).
    • Slaughter of infected animals; quarantine.
    • Protective clothing for farmers, veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers.
    • Laboratory biosafety BSL-3.
    • No human vaccine widely available.

2. Leptospirosis (Leptospira interrogans)

  • Causative organism:
    • Leptospira interrogans — spirochete; thin (0.1 µm × 6–20 µm), tightly coiled, hook-ended; actively motile.
    • >250 serovars; grouped into ~24 serogroups.
    • Common serovars in India — icterohaemorrhagiae (rats — severe Weil disease), autumnalis, australis, canicola (dogs), pomona (pigs/cattle), grippotyphosa, hebdomadis, bataviae.
  • Reservoir:
    • Rodents (rats — most important) — chronic renal carrier; shed in urine.
    • Cattle, pigs, dogs, horses, wild animals.
  • Transmission:
    • Direct contact of skin (especially abraded) or mucosa with water/soil contaminated with animal urine.
    • Occupational — farmers (rice paddies, sugarcane), sewage workers, abattoir workers, veterinarians, miners, fish farmers, military.
    • Recreational — swimming, rafting, kayaking in contaminated water.
    • Heavy rainfall & flooding — common outbreak setting (monsoon in India).
  • Incubation — 5–14 days (range 2–30 days).
  • Clinical features:
    • Biphasic illness:
      1. Leptospiraemic phase (3–7 days) — abrupt onset fever, chills, headache (severe, retro-orbital), myalgia (calf — characteristic), conjunctival suffusion (red eyes, no exudate — pathognomonic), abdominal pain, vomiting, rash; symptoms resolve temporarily.
      2. Immune phase (4–30 days) — fever returns; meningitis (aseptic); uveitis; rash; organ involvement (immune-mediated).
    • Mild form (anicteric) — most common; self-limiting; flu-like.
    • Severe form (Weil disease — icteric) — 5–10%; jaundice (hepatocellular), AKI (tubulointerstitial nephritis), pulmonary haemorrhage (life-threatening), myocarditis, multi-organ failure; mortality 10–50%.
    • Pulmonary haemorrhage — leading cause of death in severe leptospirosis; ARDS-like.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Culture — blood, CSF (first 7–10 days); urine (after 1–2 weeks); on EMJH (Ellinghausen-McCullough-Johnson-Harris) medium or Fletcher, Korthof; slow — 1–6 weeks; BSL-2.
    • Dark-field microscopy — urine, CSF; low sensitivity.
    • Serology:
      • MAT (Microscopic Agglutination Test) — gold standard; titre ≥1:800 (or 4-fold rise) significant; detects serovar-specific antibodies; live antigen; complex; reference labs only.
      • IgM ELISA — screening; sensitivity 80–90%; detects recent infection.
      • Leptadip slide agglutination — rapid; bedside.
      • Lateral flow assay — point-of-care.
    • PCR — blood, urine, CSF; early; detects DNA; serovar-specific.
    • Other tests:
      • CBG — leucocytosis, thrombocytopenia; ESR high.
      • LFT — bilirubin high (predominantly direct); AST/ALT mildly elevated (hepatocellular); AKI (raised urea, creatinine); CK elevated (myositis).
      • Urinalysis — proteinuria, haematuria, pyuria, casts.
      • Chest X-ray — pulmonary infiltrates, haemorrhage.
      • CSF — aseptic meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose).
  • Treatment:
    • Mild — Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days; OR Amoxicillin 500 mg TID × 7 days; OR Azithromycin 500 mg OD × 3 days.
    • Severe (Weil disease) — IV Penicillin G 1.5 MU 6-hourly × 7 days; OR IV Ceftriaxone 1–2 g OD × 7 days; OR IV Doxycycline + Ceftriaxone.
    • Children <8 yr — Azithromycin, Penicillin, Ceftriaxone.
    • Pregnancy — Penicillin, Ceftriaxone.
    • Supportive — IV fluids, dialysis, mechanical ventilation, blood transfusion.
    • Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction — possible with penicillin (less common than in syphilis).
    • Prophylaxis — Doxycycline 200 mg weekly for high-risk exposure.
  • Prevention:
    • Avoid contact with contaminated water — wear protective clothing, boots, gloves.
    • Rodent control.
    • Drainage of standing water; sanitation.
    • Vaccinate domestic animals (dogs, cattle).
    • Chemoprophylaxis — Doxycycline 200 mg weekly for high-risk (military, farmers, after floods).
    • Human vaccine (China, Cuba, France) — limited use.

Clinical Pearl

Brucellosis & leptospirosis are two of the most common bacterial zoonoses in India — both often undiagnosed or misdiagnosed as typhoid/malaria due to non-specific febrile presentation. Always ask about occupational & animal exposure — farmer, slaughterhouse worker, veterinarian; consumption of unpasteurised milk/cheese (brucellosis); exposure to floodwater, rice paddies, sugarcane fields, recreational swimming (leptospirosis); rat infestation (both). Brucellosis — undulant fever, sweating (malodorous), arthralgia, epididymo-orchitis, hepatosplenomegaly, sacroiliitis; blood culture (positive in 50–70%; slow — 4–6 weeks; BSL-3); SAT ≥1:160 (serology); treatment — doxycycline + rifampicin × 6 weeks. Leptospirosis — biphasic fever, severe myalgia (calf), conjunctival suffusion (red eye, no exudate — pathognomonic); Weil disease (severe — jaundice, AKI, pulmonary haemorrhage); diagnosis — MAT (gold standard) ≥1:800, IgM ELISA (screening), PCR; treatment — doxycycline (mild) or IV penicillin/ceftriaxone (severe); chemoprophylaxis with doxycycline 200 mg weekly for high-risk (military, farmers after floods). Always consider leptospirosis in any febrile patient with exposure to floodwater or animal urine — common in India's monsoon season; Mumbai, Gujarat, Kerala, Andaman outbreaks reported. Pulmonary haemorrhage is the leading cause of death in severe leptospirosis — watch for cough, haemoptysis, dyspnoea; chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates; needs ICU & mechanical ventilation.
